All three were folded into the motion, which passed 5-0 after a public hearing at which no one spoke. ### 4 — Consolidated fee schedule for building permit fees This companion resolution updates the permit fee table, which the planning director said currently comes from the 2015 International Residential Code. The categories change: one bracket is dropped and a new one added for homes above five million dollars. Staff was explicit that the goal is not more revenue — some permits will cost less and some more — and that no full-year fiscal analysis had been done, only spot checks by the finance department on sample house sizes. A member asked how a permit valuation is actually calculated and was told it is a complicated cross-reference between the permit fee schedule and the building valuation table, driven by occupancy and construction type. Another caught a one-dollar gap between the packet version and the slide; staff explained the slide was copied directly from the code council's own published table, and the error was theirs. Staff also noted the old Springbrook permitting system "is about to collapse on us," which is why the finance director has been pulled off budget work to help. The hearing drew no speakers and the resolution passed 5-0. ## Notable moments - **A whisper problem opened the meeting.** Before any business, members spent a minute wrestling with open microphones. One joked it "would be a podcast that people might consider mimes, right? Because we can't actually hear what's happening." - **A resident's homework became public input.** A member said his youngest daughter has a school assignment to write about a public improvement and wants swings at Nolen Park. He said she is nervous but he would still try to bring her to a council meeting; others encouraged it. - **Nobody spoke at either public hearing.** Both hearings on the building code and fee changes were opened and closed within the same minute, with no members of the public present to comment. - **A member owned his own voting record.** During the branding discussion he said, "I'm going to laugh because I'm going to say it was a 4-1 vote every single time," adding that his objection had always been the money and conceding much of the work was probably needed anyway. - **Who picks the public art.** A member asked what stops staff from choosing art the council would not support once the money is allocated. The answer was that procurement rules require the selection to come back to council for approval before it is funded: "they're not going to run out and just pick a project and say we're done." - **An off-agenda road got planted as a seed.** A member described a quarter-mile connection behind the rodeo grounds that would tie into the new traffic signal, then admitted it was outside the topic: "I'm just kind of planting that seed because it's nothing that we're going to fund right now." Staff noted a deed restriction on the park side may complicate it. - **A tractor with no replacement plan.** Asked when the city's Kubota tractor — used across departments and reportedly in rough shape — would be replaced, staff conceded no depreciation or replacement schedule was ever built for it. ## About this transcript The audio was produced by automatic speech-to-text, and several proper nouns are clearly mangled. "Point Express" is Pony Express, "Sintla" and "Sitla" are the state trust lands agency SITLA, "utility cell proceeds" is almost certainly utility sale proceeds, "TSD" is likely TDS (total dissolved solids), and "CMO" is likely a certificate of occupancy. "Nolan Park" is rendered here as Nolen Park. The park named "Brandon Park" in the transcript is uncertain — it may be a substitution of a staff member's first name — so it is described by location here instead. Names appearing only once, including a fire district reviewer and a third-party code consultant, are not reproduced because the spelling could not be confirmed. Speaker attribution is the main limitation. The work session has no roll call, and most speakers are not named as they talk, so nearly all of the budget discussion is attributed to "a member" unless someone was addressed by name — Melissa Clark, Jared Gray and Wright are the exceptions. The regular meeting's two roll calls are reliable and record Clark, Burnham, Wood, Wright and Gray as the five voting members, which is a different council lineup than the city's current one; a former member, Curtis, is referred to in the past tense. The mayor presides throughout but is never named on the recording, so no name is given here. There is a stretch in the rodeo arena discussion where several sentences about a storage shed repeat verbatim four or five times — a transcription loop, not five separate statements. Elapsed times in the meeting map are estimates based on position in the transcript; the only clock times spoken aloud are 5:13, 5:15 and 5:16, near the end.

docs.title: City Council Meeting — 2024-10-29 (minutes not yet published)
docs.text: Meeting of 2024-10-29. The minutes for this meeting have not been published yet, so the site has no motion list or roll-call record for it — the account below comes from the meeting recording and its transcript. **In short:** Eagle Mountain's council and staff sat down with regional planners for a briefing on the Transit Fresh Look study, a joint effort by eight cities and several transportation agencies to plan new transit for northern Utah County and southwest Salt Lake County. No decisions were made. The city's representatives pushed back hard on the draft route maps, arguing the plan bypasses the Ranches and ignores Pioneer Crossing, and the consultants agreed to revisit those lines. **Present:** The transcript does not record a roll call, so individual attendance cannot be confirmed. Elected officials and city staff spoke throughout, but the recording does not identify them by name. **Staff:** Lauren Victor (long-range planner, Wasatch Front Regional Council — attending remotely because of illness); Liz Scanlon (Kimley-Horn, the consultant firm facilitating the study, presenting the slides). ## Decisions *No motions were voted on.* **Settled without a vote:** - The consultants agreed to take Eagle Mountain's objection back to the project team and re-examine whether the main east-west corridor should follow the lakefront alignment or Pioneer Crossing, after city representatives said the current draft skips the Ranches entirely. - The consultants acknowledged the concern that a route along 2100 North functions as a freeway and would not attract riders, and said they would "go back and talk that out" alongside suggestions for Pony Express and Porter Rockwell. - The consultants accepted that a proposed yellow line should be extended to reach the American Fork FrontRunner station, which the current map does not show. - No direction was given on corridor width preservation beyond the consultants' commitment to work through right-of-way constraints with city staff over the following weeks. ## Meeting map | Agenda ref | Topic | ~Start (elapsed) | One-line note | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | — | Introductions and remote-participation setup | 0:00 | Presenters introduced themselves; one joined online because of a cold. | | — | Transit Fresh Look study: purpose, partnership, and process | 0:03 | Overview of the eight-city study, its four phases, and its goals. | | — | Transit-oriented development and the "five D's" | 0:12 | Density, distance, design, diversity of land uses, and destinations. | | — | Corridor mapping: where the study stands | 0:18 | Draft Utah County corridor map, performance measures, and next steps. | | — | Land use, city influence, and mode types | 0:26 | What cities control versus what regional agencies control. | | — | Questions and discussion | 0:34 | Corridor preservation, phasing, and objections to the draft alignments. | **Discussed but NOT on the agenda:** Because no agenda was available for this record, nothing can be identified as off-agenda. After the formal presentation ended, the recording captures informal side conversation about housing costs and price per square foot that appears to be unrelated chatter rather than city business. **On agenda but little/no discussion:** Cannot be determined — no agenda was available for this meeting. ## What was discussed ### Transit Fresh Look — study purpose and partnership The meeting was a briefing on the Transit Fresh Look study, a regional planning effort to work out what it would take to bring more transit into southwest Salt Lake County and northern Utah County. Liz Scanlon of Kimley-Horn, the consulting firm facilitating the work, explained that the study deliberately steps back from past efforts. "We know that transit has been studied and talked about a lot, and there might be a little bit of fatigue about that," she said, but the team is "endeavoring to kind of step back and bring new thoughts to the table." The study is run as a partnership rather than a top-down plan. The contract sits with the Wasatch Front Regional Council, but the partners include the Mountainland Association of Governments, the Utah Department of Transportation, the Utah Transit Authority, and eight cities: Lehi, Saratoga Springs, Bluffdale, South Jordan, Herriman, Riverton, Eagle Mountain, and West Jordan. Scanlon stressed repeatedly that the consultants would not push a conclusion the cities did not share: "if there's not feeling good or there's not good vibes or we're just a little bit nervous, we really want to understand that." The work runs in four stages — diagnostic, discovery, refining, and blueprint. The team started under contract in April with data collection on existing conditions and city land use plans, held a brainstorming session in July where participants drew lines on maps, and met again in September to narrow those ideas into corridors. The next partners meeting was set for November 18, with the blueprint stage — a roadmap for how to actually build any of this — coming in the new year. ### Goals and transit-oriented development Scanlon walked through the goals the partners set at the outset: better connections within the valley and to the wider region, improved access for people who struggle to get around, economic development that fits each city's own general plan, and above all a plan that gets used. There was, she said, "a really, really important emphasis on an implementable plan. Like not a planning study we throw on a shelf." She then explained the ingredients of transit-oriented development, which she grouped as density, distance, design, diversity of land uses, and destinations. She was careful to defuse the word density: "we're not talking about high rises and anything inappropriate," she said, but rather modest development — ground-floor shops with a couple of storeys of housing above — clustered near stations. She also flagged uses that work against transit, naming car washes and gas stations as poor neighbours for a transit line, and suggested cities think about what happens as those properties turn over. A recurring theme was the split in control. Cities control zoning, where development goes, and station access — sidewalks and bike connections. Regional agencies control service types and frequency. The goal, she said, is transit that beats driving: "I can ride the transit vehicle and get on Wi-Fi or get on my phone and work or read a book or sleep versus sitting on I-15 in traffic." ### Corridor maps and mode choice The presentation included a draft Utah County corridor map that Scanlon described as "hot off the press" and headed to the November partners meeting. The lines were scored against performance measures drawn partly from federal funding criteria, since new transit in the region has historically depended on federal money, and partly on access to FrontRunner, future land use, and rough cost and feasibility. She was blunt about the limits of the exercise at this stage: "we don't want to set you up for failure to the degree that, gosh, we drew a line and it has to go across Utah Lake." The next phase moves from where the lines go to what runs on them. The study will weigh local bus, bus rapid transit, and light rail. Scanlon described bus rapid transit as "light rail light" — a bus with dedicated stations, sometimes its own guideway, branded vehicles and off-board fare collection, similar to the UVX service in Orem and Provo. Light rail is far more expensive; a fixed-route bus is the cheapest starting point. ### Questions from the body The first question asked whether the study looked at corridor widths that need to be preserved not just for bus rapid transit but for future light rail. Scanlon answered "yes and no" — the team has collected what cities have already preserved, and is only now starting detailed right-of-way conversations with city staff. A speaker in the room pressed the point sharply: "The most expensive part of transit is the land," and buying corridors in the wrong place wastes taxpayer money, while waiting means tearing down homes and businesses later. "So the sooner we can get that, the better." A second question asked whether the study is looking at what has to be built first — whether the routes have a sequence, or would be built piecemeal wherever pressure appears. Scanlon said phasing discussion started in September and is common practice: build a fast bus, watch ridership grow, upgrade to bus rapid transit, and eventually light rail, while preserving the corridor from the start. She singled out Eagle Mountain as offering "a really amazing opportunity here to align general plan, zoning and land use in these transit corridors together." She also corrected an assumption from the floor that a central corridor project is under construction — the grey line on the map covers corridors under construction *or* with a locally preferred alternative selected, which is a stage of study, not a shovel in the ground. ### The Pioneer Crossing and Ranches objection The sharpest exchange came over what the draft map leaves out. A speaker noted that at a staff meeting the previous month, Pioneer Crossing had shown as the highest-ranking corridor, and asked why it no longer appears. Others in the room piled on: Pony Express has a gap through the Ranches, and the high-capacity route as drawn bypasses the Ranches completely, running down Ranches Parkway instead. "There's thousands of cars coming through Saratoga Springs on Pony Express," one speaker said. "I would love to see some of those people on buses, but this is showing the high capacity route, bypassing the ranches completely." The frustration was partly about money already spent. "We got $1.3 billion to fix Pioneer Crossing and there's not even no kind of plan for bus rapid transit," a speaker said, calling the map "so confusing" given that Pioneer Crossing is the busiest road. Another objected to routing transit on 2100 North on the grounds that it is effectively a freeway, and freeway buses lose: "People don't want to take the bus when they're sitting on the bus on a freeway and people are going past them 80 miles an hour in a car." The alternative offered was a route that beats congestion rather than joins it — "if you're on Pioneer Crossing and you're going on a bus and you're passing everyone who's in gridlock traffic, you're like, oh yeah, I'm doing right." Scanlon explained how the map got that way. After July's brainstorm, the team ran performance measures on the ideas, then re-workshopped the lines at the September partners meeting, and this map came out of that discussion. She acknowledged the lakefront-versus-Pioneer-Crossing question "was a whole lot of debate in that meeting" with Utah County city representatives and remains unsettled. She also explained the Mountain View Corridor line: Salt Lake County partners see a large gap in north-south transit between I-15 and the west side, and want to know where such a line could connect in Utah County — potentially at an intermodal hub in Saratoga Springs feeding the Eagle Mountain lines. On Pioneer Crossing, she conceded the point: "I appreciate the comment that maybe we don't have this line quite right... We'll go back and talk that out." ## Notable moments - **A remote presenter and muffled audio.** Lauren Victor of the Wasatch Front Regional Council attended online after coming down with a cold, and warned early that the room came through "a little muffled when there's multiple people talking" — a caveat that shows up in the recording as well. - **"It's both with 200,000 people."** When Scanlon framed the choice as lakefront *or* Pioneer Crossing, a speaker rejected the either/or outright, citing the combined population of Eagle Mountain and Saratoga Springs as reason for both. - **A correction on the central corridor.** A speaker opened by saying they were "thrilled that the central corridor is under construction." Victor stepped in to clarify that the grey line on the map covers corridors under construction *or* with a locally preferred alternative, and that construction should not be assumed. - **The land-cost warning.** The most forceful contribution of the night was not a question but a statement: preserving the same corridors and alignments across all the cities matters now, because "the last thing we need to do is build a bunch more houses and businesses that are going to have to get torn down." - **A missing FrontRunner connection.** Scanlon volunteered that the map does not quite show what the partners agreed in September — a yellow line "should probably get to the American Fork FrontRunner Station." ## About this transcript The automatic transcription garbles several proper nouns. "Kimley Horne" and "Kim Lee Horn" both stand for Kimley-Horn, the consulting firm; "Lehigh" is Lehi; "Hermann" is Herriman; "Meg" is almost certainly MAG, the Mountainland Association of Governments; "EVX" is UVX, the Utah Valley Express bus rapid transit line; and "quarters" appears repeatedly where the speaker said "corridors." The word "fair media" is likely "fare media." Speaker attribution is very limited. The recording contains no roll call and almost no names, so with the exception of the two presenters — Lauren Victor and Liz Scanlon, who introduced themselves — it is not possible to say which elected official or staff member made any given comment. Questions and objections during the discussion are therefore attributed only to "a speaker." Because no agenda was available for this meeting, the meeting map is reconstructed from the flow of the recording and the elapsed times are rough estimates. Audio quality degrades badly in two places. A stretch near the end of the presentation is unintelligible, with a phrase about shutting down "the point of the street" repeating several times in a way that does not resolve into meaning. After the presenters signed off, the recording continues to capture informal conversation about housing prices, square-foot costs, and unrelated small talk that is fragmentary and largely incoherent; none of it has been treated as city business.

docs.title: City Council Meeting — 2024-11-14 (minutes not yet published)
docs.text: Meeting of 2024-11-14. The minutes for this meeting have not been published yet, so the site has no motion list or roll-call record for it — the account below comes from the meeting recording and its transcript. **In short:** This was day one of the city council's two‑day strategic planning conference — a working session, not a regular meeting, so nothing was formally voted on. Staff walked the council through new asset‑management software, progress on the city's 2022 goals, housing and population numbers, a facilities wish list and a new economic development strategy. The council's recurring theme was that departments are stretched too thin and that residents are not being told what the city is already doing. **Present:** Mayor Jared Gray; Councilmembers Melissa Clark, Brett Wright and Rich Wood are identifiable by name in the recording. No roll call was taken, so the transcript does not confirm whether Councilmembers Craig Whiting and Zac Huish were in the room. **Staff:** Steve (city administrator), Cliff (presented the goals and objectives update), Brad (public works, presented the asset‑management software), Zac Hilton (parks and public works operations), Brandon (planning, presented growth and housing), Evan (economic development), Kimberly (finance), Tyler (communications), Natalie and Terrence (facilities planning presentation), Angela (human resources), Michelle (library), Vince (engineering), Marcus (city attorney). Also referenced but not clearly speaking: Todd Black (wildlife biologist, becoming open space manager), Trevor and Todd (utility locates), Brody (public works), Dustin (building), Paula (neighborhood improvement office staff). ## Decisions *No motions were voted on.* **Settled without a vote:** - The council told public works to stop absorbing the software data‑entry burden in‑house and to come back asking for contract help, interns or new positions, rather than having directors spend whole weeks on it. - The council agreed the highest‑priority city facilities are the wastewater treatment plant expansion, an office building tied to that plant, a new city hall built together with a library, and buying land now for everything else. - A standalone recreation center was pushed down the priority list, with agreement that if it is pursued it should go to voters as a bond question accompanied by real cost figures. - The council agreed the existing city hall should be converted into the public safety building once a new city hall is built, subject to staff confirming what building standards that conversion would require. - Staff were asked to bring financing options and land‑acquisition costs for the top facility priorities to the first council meeting in January, not December, so the council sees the full picture at once. - Finance was asked to study how far the city's 35 percent reserve floor could safely be lowered to fund staffing, and to pair any recommendation with a plan for rebuilding the reserve. - The council endorsed economic development's three target industries — life sciences, energy and cyber, and aerospace and defense — and asked for written proposals on a downtown zone and a retail approval overlay. - Staff were directed to address full‑scale nuclear generation in the alternative energy code already being drafted, alongside gas plants, small modular reactors and solar. - The mayor agreed to send councilmembers his list of proposed topic committees so the group could discuss it the next day and again at an upcoming council meeting. - Planning was asked to come back with how many vested units have actually been built, broken down by housing type, and with the equivalent figures from prior years for comparison. - Planning and communications agreed to publicize a low‑cost permitting path for basement apartments that were never permitted, both to help residents at resale and to improve the city's utility‑demand data. - The council asked to be notified before citywide surveys or major messages go out, so members are not hearing about them first from residents. - The cemetery building was deferred to a three‑to‑five‑year window, timed to the next phase of grave sites. - The parks, planning, library, treasurer, special events and water sections of the goals document were set aside for a later wrap‑up rather than walked through. ## Meeting map | Agenda ref | Topic | ~Start (elapsed) | One-line note | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Welcome and framing of the conference | ~0:00 | Mayor read the dictionary definition of "strategy" and asked for a high‑level day. | | 2 | Asset and work‑order software demonstration | ~0:05 | Public works showed sewer, manhole and utility‑locate tracking now running live. | | 3 | Status update on strategic goals and objectives | ~1:00 | 24 of 111 actions complete; turned into a wide‑ranging debate on priorities and staffing. | | 3a | Weeds, neighborhood cleanup and volunteers | ~1:35 | Council pushed for a volunteer program and better publicity of work already done. | | 3b | Communications, branding and economic development incentives | ~2:00 | "What is Eagle Mountain's brand?" left as an open question for staff. | | 3c | Power supply and data centers | ~2:10 | Data centers stalled for lack of power; council wants its own generation options studied. | | 3d | Engineering standards and stormwater deficiencies | ~2:25 | Existing flood‑prone areas to get a deficiency master plan alongside the growth plans. | | 3e | Finance, reserves and staffing costs | ~2:35 | Council signalled willingness to draw down reserves to hire. | | — | Break | ~2:45 | | | 4 | Housing and population growth update | ~2:50 | 16,252 households today; roughly 40,000 vested or platted units on the books. | | — | Lunch and staff team‑building games | ~4:00 | Baby‑photo guessing game and a quiz app; no city business. | | 5 | Facilities master plan prioritization exercise | ~4:45 | Council sorted buildings into high, medium and low priority on a board. | | 6 | Economic development strategy | ~6:30 | New approach built on target industries, zoning changes and third‑party data. | | 7 | Wrap‑up and setup for the annexation discussion | ~7:45 | Southern annexation overlapping Saratoga Springs held for the next day. | **Discussed but NOT on the agenda:** renting versus buying mobile office units for overflow staff; the condition of the right‑of‑way left behind by the Cedar Pass pipeline contractor; a request that the governor be invited to a separate meeting about power; and the overlapping southern annexation with Saratoga Springs, which was deliberately held over to the second day. **On agenda but little/no discussion:** the parks, planning, treasurer's office, special events, cemetery and water sections of the goals document were skipped because the council felt they had already been covered in other conversations; the attorney and library sections drew only passing comment. ## What was discussed ### 2 — Asset and work‑order software Public works demonstrated the asset‑management software the council funded roughly a year ago, which the city is using to catalogue everything it owns and every hour of work done on it. Staff said the mapping now covers 4,817 segments of sewer pipe — a segment being the run between two manholes — and 4,291 manholes, with about 187 miles of sewer main. Every vehicle and piece of equipment is loaded with an hourly cost rate drawn from federal disaster‑reimbursement rates, and every employee has a rate based on the midpoint of their pay band rather than their actual salary, so nobody's pay is exposed. The payoff staff highlighted was the utility‑locate queue. Because the system now talks directly to the 811 "blue stakes" call line, one inspector has cleared 6,364 locate requests since the end of May with only 13 outstanding, and can close tickets without driving to sites where the city has no buried utilities. In the same period crews jetted 564 pipe segments — nearly 25 miles — at a tracked cost of $25,084, and completed 629 manhole inspections at $2,563, flagging 12 manholes for closer watching. The council's questions were less about the software than about who does the work. Told that the director had spent whole weeks on data entry, members said plainly that was the wrong use of his time and pressed him to ask for contractors, interns or new staff. One councilmember asked how the city would ever catch up on assets built before the system existed; the answer was that new development would be captured through engineering inspections and GIS as a matter of routine, but the backlog had no good answer yet. Members also asked whether jetting and inspection costs are being recovered in utility rates, and urged the city to tell residents this story as evidence of efficiency. ### 3 — Status update on strategic goals and objectives Staff reminded the council that the 2022 strategic plan produced six goals, which staff turned into 37 objectives and 111 actions assigned across departments. Five months into the fiscal year, 24 actions are at 100 percent and about ten more are near 75 percent, with six not measured — some because no good measure exists, others because the engineering department's two most senior people are brand new. Staff described the current two‑year cycle as "the year of capital asset management," with technology as the second theme, and said most measures are completion‑based rather than statistical because so many of the actions amount to installing a program. The presentation turned into an argument about the council's own role. Members said the objectives were written by staff without them, which leaves the council unable to judge whether the work actually advances the goals, and warned that the objectives list collides with the separate legislative priority list — the same three departments are being asked to do both. "If we don't know what those things are, then we are part of the problem," one member said. Another cut in more bluntly: the council was spending its limited time discussing the template rather than the content, and wanted to ask department by department what is stuck at 10 percent and why. Smaller items surfaced along the way. The library reported four of six planned new programs launched, physical circulation growth already at target and digital use up 9.8 percent against a 25 percent goal, and explained that $2,000 buys roughly 300 physical items but only about 77 digital ones, many of them leased rather than owned. Facilities noted that operating costs rise as buildings age. Staff said an artificial intelligence policy has been adopted and that other Utah cities are already using such tools for budget documents and procurement drafting. ### 3a — Weeds, neighborhood cleanup and volunteers A councilmember recounted a veteran asking him at a breakfast what it would take to get the city's weeds under control, and floated the man's own suggestion: let organizations adopt sections of the city. The council pushed hard on the idea that the city has, as one member put it, 72,000 potential volunteers if it will organize them — providing equipment, dumpsters and disposal while residents supply the labor. Staff said two trailers and equipment have already been purchased for exactly this purpose, and that cleanup work can extend onto private and homeowners‑association property with permission. Two obstacles were named. The first is continuity: the last big volunteer push, roughly nine years ago, drew over 700 people but depended on one staff member who has since moved on, and the annual volunteer group now rotates so often that nobody knows who is running it. Members said one person should own this permanently. The second is liability. The attorney's view was that a risk assessment should be quick and that if the city goes far down the liability road it may as well hire people instead; a councilmember countered that the city should accept the risk and use volunteers. Staff also pushed back on the premise that nothing is being done. Todd Black is moving into a new open space manager role alongside his wildlife biologist duties, with an approved technician to support him, and crews have sprayed thistle along trails and corridors and are testing four seed mixes, including pollinator mixes, on detention ponds and at city hall. The council's response was that this was news to them, which proved the communications point: "we're not getting that message out." ### 3b — Communications, branding and economic development incentives Councilmembers asked to be told before surveys and major messages go out, not because they want editorial control but because residents call them about things they have not seen. Someone also suggested mailing a monthly event calendar with utility bills, on the argument that residents over roughly 50 who do not follow the city's social media are missing everything. The branding discussion came out of a planning commission meeting where commissioners could not articulate what Eagle Mountain's brand is. Members agreed the substance is outdoors, trails, open space and wildlife, but had no short way to say it — "Springville City is the art city; how do we describe ourselves?" The related question was whether the brand, the general plan and the strategic plan are actually pulling in the same direction, and one member asked pointedly whether anyone has ever checked. On the economic development incentive policy, staff explained it exists so the city has a consistent way to evaluate requests from incoming industry rather than negotiating from scratch each time. Council members said the policy should be a standard worksheet capturing jobs, investment and timing rather than a restrictive cap, and argued the city's strongest incentive is non‑financial: cheap land, lots of it, and a workforce of 72,000 people who would rather drive 15 minutes than an hour. ### 3c — Power supply and data centers This was the most urgent conversation of the day. The council was told that data center projects are stalling for lack of electricity, and one member who had championed the projects said the situation makes him "a lot more nervous" about the positions he originally took. Because the school district's finances depend heavily on data center revenue, the risk extends well beyond the city. The scale was put in perspective by a comment that one of the city's data centers would use more power than the entire state of Wyoming. Members floated building the city's own generation — nuclear, natural gas, or otherwise — and, as a secondary idea, buying the distribution system back from Rocky Mountain Power. The obstacles described were regulatory rather than technical: Rocky Mountain Power effectively holds a monopoly on transmission, and legislators have told the city that both state and federal action would be needed to clear a path for independent generation and new transmission lines. Requests have already come in for 300 acres for a large nuclear plant and from two natural gas developers. The council asked economic development to gather what data exists on each generation type — output, footprint, and effects on residents, wildlife and neighboring communities — so members can decide what the city is willing to accept and where. They also asked that public education come before controversy, since outside groups typically arrive to shape opinion once a power project is announced. A legislators' breakfast was scheduled for the next morning, and members wanted a separate meeting arranged with federal delegation members and the governor. ### 3d — Engineering standards and stormwater Council members asked engineering to re‑examine the city's construction standards — roads, backfill, collapsible soils, utilities — not merely against state minimums but against what actually holds up locally, and asked to be told where the city is under‑engineered today so those fixes can be budgeted rather than repeated. They also asked that new applications come with an explicit statement of their impact on sewer, water and stormwater capacity, so approvals are not granted without knowing the consequence. Stormwater dominated. Staff described Cedar Pass Ranch as having essentially no drainage, with much of it platted before the city existed, and said the same is true of most areas without curb and gutter or backing onto hillsides. The deficiencies are too large to fix in‑house, so a master plan for existing problems is being commissioned alongside the master plans for future growth — with the point made that deficiency work is not impact‑fee eligible and needs a separate funding answer. Staff have already mapped problem areas by severity and extent to find low‑cost, high‑damage fixes first. The council's insistence was that specific known trouble spots be fixed before the master plan is finished, naming a Valley View pipe already upsized to the detention pond, a resident who spent about $19,000 replacing a basement, flooding near a church parking lot that originates on private property, and an undersized pipe that floods the Bell Street area near a school. "If it happens again because we haven't acted, then shame on us." A stormwater rate proposal was set for the following Tuesday with adoption targeted for December 3. ### 3e — Finance, reserves and staffing Asked whether revenue is tracking to projection, the finance director said the city is on target but that only two months of sales tax have been reported, because state distributions run two months behind. A councilmember pressed the real question: with every department signalling it needs more people, is the city heading into its reserves again next year? The answer was that using reserves for ongoing operating costs is possible and already happening through budget amendments, but is not recommended, and that whether it is sustainable depends entirely on when new revenue — Walmart, the data centers — actually arrives. The council asked finance to study whether the 35 percent reserve floor could come down to 30 or 25 percent, what that would buy in staffing, and how the fund would be rebuilt. Members also said openly that a modest property tax increase has to be part of the conversation, with one warning against repeating the county's mistake of holding rates flat for decades and then facing a large correction. "We shouldn't have to fund what we do on the backs of our employees." That led into a long exchange on retention. Members asked department heads to identify the specific individuals the city cannot afford to lose and get their pay addressed now, arguing it is cheaper than replacing them, and asked human resources to fix baseline pay so positions do not sit open for months. A separate thread argued that the deeper problem is job design — people carrying two or three roles at once — and that the city should split those duties into properly staffed positions. As one member put it, "we're mediocre in our job because I have too many jobs." ### 4 — Housing and population growth Planning presented the city's own count: 16,252 residential building permits, plus permitted accessory dwelling units, which staff use to rebut state population estimates they consider two years stale. Staff said the Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute is expected to work with the city on a method that fits Eagle Mountain's growth pattern and could be replicated elsewhere. Building permits are running about 1,190 residential this year with two months left, against a low of 868 during the pandemic and inflation dip, and several builders are gearing up for more. The numbers that drew the most attention were the vested ones. Of the city's 52 square miles, roughly 30 are already vested, leaving about 20 to plan — and most of what remains is designated for business, industrial or commercial use rather than housing. There are about 23,000 vested but unbuilt units, and roughly 40,000 counting platted lots, which would put the city near 160,000 to 175,000 residents at build‑out. Platted lots alone would support close to 76,000 people. Growth is now overwhelmingly in the south, at 17.4 percent against 1.7 percent in the north. A councilmember pressed the point that although more than 80 percent of built housing is single‑family detached, this year's permits are about 73 percent single‑family and the vested pipeline trends toward a 70‑30 split. The argument was that the "missing middle" the state says the city lacks is in fact already entitled and simply not being built fast enough by developers, and the council should stop planning as though today's inventory is the future. Members asked for built‑versus‑vested figures by housing type, and prior‑year slide decks for comparison. Two side threads came out of this. First, accessory dwelling units rose from 115 to 134, are not separately metered, and cannot be charged impact fees when they are internal to a home under state law — which staff said pushes infrastructure costs onto ratepayers and is a live concern at the regional sewer district. The council discussed an amnesty‑style outreach encouraging owners of unpermitted basement apartments to get permitted cheaply, both to help them at resale and to improve the city's data. Second, members asked whether the city can require builders to finish one development before starting another; the attorney's answer was that the city cannot condition an application on a developer's other projects, but is never obligated to rezone, and can decline on the merits — including that a proposal would create an isolated "utility island." ### 5 — Facilities master plan prioritization Facilities staff walked through which buildings the city needs, which would require buying land, and roughly what each would cost, then ran a live exercise in which the council sorted them into high, medium and low priority. High priority came out as the wastewater treatment plant expansion, an office building constructed with it, a new city hall, and — added by the council as its own category — land acquisition for everything on the list. Staff clarified that the plant expansion under discussion takes capacity from 2.4 to 4.8 million gallons a day, one of three eventual phases, not the full build‑out. The council's strongest instinct was to buy land now. "If we don't secure the land for some of these things for a full build‑out scenario, we're going to be kicking ourselves," one member said, arguing that what costs a few million today will cost far more later. A related argument was made for the satellite public works site on the north end: rather than a salt shed, the city should buy enough ground now to build a real base of operations for a city of 175,000, even if only a storage yard is built initially. Public safety was settled quickly. Because the existing city hall was designed with a holding cell, a separate entrance and a concrete basement, the council decided it should become the police building once a new city hall is built, buying years of time — subject to staff confirming how much retrofitting current standards would require, since hardened public safety buildings are held to a higher construction standard than ordinary offices. The recreation center produced the day's sharpest disagreement, and it was about governance rather than swimming. Several members said residents are asking for recreation, that demand has grown with the influx of younger families, and that the question should go to voters as a bond. One member said she would not vote for it herself but would support putting it on the ballot; another objected that a ballot measure lets some residents impose a tax on neighbors on fixed incomes for something that is not a basic government function, and noted that Lehi's center runs about two million dollars a year in the red even after doubling rates. The compromise reached was to separate "recreation opportunities" from "a recreation center" — a pond, ice skating, an inflatable dome over existing courts, classroom space in a combined city hall and library — and to pursue those cheaper options first, with any center going to voters accompanied by real cost figures. A design already exists from before the pandemic. Members also asked staff to think in phases and timeframes rather than full price tags — high priority meaning work starts now with results in five years, and so on — and asked for financing options, not just land prices, before deciding. Staff noted that combining a city hall with a library could save $10 to $15 million and tends to poll better with residents, and that Saratoga Springs built at just under $50 million while leasing a floor to the county health department for eight to ten years. ### 6 — Economic development strategy Economic development opened with the argument that the field has changed: site selection is now overwhelmingly data‑driven, location visits come last, and national retailers disregard a city's own figures in favor of third‑party models. Staff said neither the state economic development office nor the statewide recruiting nonprofit represents Eagle Mountain accurately despite being given good information, and that long‑standing relationships steer prospects toward established cities before Eagle Mountain gets a look. Three approaches were proposed. First, zoning and approvals: a genuine downtown zone that keeps ground‑floor space for uses that draw people rather than insurance and dental offices, plus a retail equivalent of the existing technology overlay so approved uses in targeted areas can be handled at staff level — because retailers hate repeated entitlement rounds as much as they dislike cost. Second, industrial name recognition: pick specific industries, market the city's land and workforce for them consistently, and have every elected official and staff member telling the same story. Third, buying a commercial data tool such as Placer.ai or Buxton so the city can bring recent third‑party figures on where residents shop, work and travel. The three proposed target industries were life sciences, energy and cyber, and aerospace and defense. Staff argued life sciences pays well, has decades of growth ahead and includes companies currently dissatisfied with their space elsewhere; that a power generation facility brings a highly skilled workforce which in turn attracts unrelated high‑tech employers; and that secure facilities tend to follow data centers. Councilmembers accepted all three while pressing to also court outdoor‑gear and bicycle manufacturers as a natural fit for the city's brand — the suggestion being a "brand overlay" that eases approvals for businesses that reinforce what the city is trying to be. Members also asked about attracting the software and e‑commerce employers concentrated in Lehi and Draper; staff's view was that those will follow rather than lead, and suggested a flexible shared‑office model as a nearer‑term option. On retail, Walmart is under construction with a summer or fall 2025 opening, several pad sites are moving at Porter's Crossing and the marketplace, and mid‑box and regional stores — a home improvement chain, a fitness chain, movie theaters — have all been approached but are struggling to make construction costs work. Staff said one commercial tract along the boulevard is not selling despite heavy traffic counts, because the models being used do not capture nearby development. The council asked how success will be measured and how quickly the strategy would be revisited if it does not produce jobs and tax base, and asked staff to return with an evaluation method and a demonstration of the data tool before any purchase. ## Notable moments - **A resident's suggestion drove the volunteer discussion.** A councilmember relayed a veteran's question at a veterans' breakfast — what will it take to control the weeds — and the man's own answer, that organizations should adopt sections of the city. The council spent nearly half an hour on it. - **The council told staff, repeatedly, to ask for help.** "If it's a consultant group that can get it done in a month, so we're up and going instead of waiting for it to be nine months or 18 months from now, please ask." - **A direct challenge to the format of the session.** One member interrupted the goals presentation to say the group was spending its time on the template rather than the content: "if we're going to have a strategic planning, we need to talk about what's in this." - **A reversal on data centers.** A member who had been "a super big advocate" for the projects, partly on behalf of school district finances, said the power shortage now makes him far more nervous about that position. - **Open disagreement on putting a rec center to a vote.** One member said she would put it on the ballot and vote against it personally; another argued a ballot measure means letting some residents tax neighbors on fixed incomes for something that is not a basic government service. Both positions were stated plainly and neither was resolved. - **The attorney was blunt about developer accountability.** Asked whether the city could withhold approval from a builder who had not finished an earlier project, he said the city can always decline to rezone and can say, "we're not comfortable that you're actually going to be able to carry out your promises." - **A staff member was asked to speak up more.** Engineering was told directly: "when we're in these meetings and you hear us saying stuff and we don't understand the full impact, that's when you take a little mic and say, I'd like to say something." - **The middle of the day was social.** Lunch included a baby‑photo guessing game and a quiz app about staff and elected officials; no city business was conducted during it. - **The day ended on an unfinished item.** An overlapping southern annexation next to Saratoga Springs, roughly 162 acres, was raised at the close and deliberately held for the second day so the council could agree a position — particularly on street connections — before meeting with the neighboring city. ## About this transcript The audio was transcribed automatically and several proper nouns are unreliable. The asset‑management software is OpenGov (Cartegraph), rendered variously as "OpenRove" and "open gov." The Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute appears as "Kim Gardner," "Kenzie Gardner" and "CHEM‑C." Cory Wride Memorial Park appears as "Corey Wright," "Corey Gray," "Corydive" and "quarry ride." Pony Express Parkway appears as "Point Express" and "Cochrane Express." The data center operator QTS appears as "GTS," and a third developer is rendered "TRAC" (most likely Tract). Other unclear names include the pipeline contractor ("Beanie Bush" / "BD Bush"), a developer rendered "Al Rafferty," the city toured by economic development staff (rendered "Pace"), and a homebuilder rendered "Fulte" (Pulte). Stormwater permits are referred to as "SWIP," almost certainly SWPPP. "Blue stakes" refers to the 811 utility‑locate service, and TSSD is the regional sewer district. Speaker attribution is the biggest limitation. There was no roll call and the recording does not label speakers, so most remarks are quoted here without a name. Where a name appears, it is because someone in the room used it aloud — which is why Mayor Gray and Councilmembers Clark, Wright and Wood can be identified and the other two councilmembers cannot. Note also that "Zach" throughout the day refers to a staff member over parks and public works, not to Councilmember Zac Huish. Audio is unclear in several stretches: the opening minutes of the software presentation contain a long garbled repetition; the lunch break, the photo‑guessing game and the quiz activity are largely unintelligible and contain no city business; and the final two minutes trail off mid‑conversation about the next day's agenda. Some figures were explicitly flagged as provisional by staff — the sewer mileage in particular — and should not be treated as final.

docs.title: City Council Meeting — 2024-11-15 (minutes not yet published)
docs.text: Meeting of 2024-11-15. The minutes for this meeting have not been published yet, so the site has no motion list or roll-call record for it — the account below comes from the meeting recording and its transcript. **In short:** This was the council's annual strategic planning retreat, held at the Chamber of Commerce with a state lawmaker, the mayor and a councilmember from Saratoga Springs, and two school board members joining at different points. No votes were taken. The council agreed to tell Saratoga Springs in writing that it will not fight a 162-acre annexation next door — while putting its traffic and child-safety worries on the record — and asked staff to merge the city's goal list with its list of pending tasks. **Present:** Mayor Jared Gray (left before the end and listened in by phone from the road); Councilmembers Melissa Clark, Brett Wright, Rich Wood, and a councilmember the transcript calls Donna. No roll call was taken, so this list reflects only the members heard by name. **Staff:** Cliff (legislative affairs director), Steve (community development and planning), Marcus (city attorney), and a contract lobbyist the recording renders as both "Mr. Stewart" and "Mr. Stern." **Guests:** Representative Stephanie Gricius (Utah House); Jim Miller (mayor, Saratoga Springs) and a Saratoga Springs councilmember; Julie and Joylin (Alpine School District board members, by video). ## Decisions *No motions were voted on.* **Settled without a vote:** - The council agreed to have the city attorney draft a letter telling Saratoga Springs that Eagle Mountain does not intend to protest the annexation, while stating serious concerns about road connections and the safety of children walking to nearby schools, and recording the two councils' shared understanding that the land is meant for single-family homes. - Members agreed they would not keep pushing to move the new high school off the site now under contract, and would instead work on how future school sites get chosen. - The council accepted a school board member's offer to hold a long planning session in March with each city — Eagle Mountain and Saratoga Springs separately — to map where schools should go over the next several decades. - Staff was directed to merge the legislative priorities list with the strategic plan's objectives, break the combined list out by department, send it to members electronically, and begin working through it one department at a time starting two weeks from the following Tuesday, beginning with planning, which carries the most items. - Cliff was asked to produce a shortened version of the priorities list — item titles and one line each — and to consider posting it as a view-only live document so it does not have to be re-emailed after every update. - On committees, the council agreed not to create everything on the two lists brought forward, to start small and let successful ones grow, and that annexation and power generation are the two most urgent. - Representative Gricius agreed to ask Senator Brammer why the new district's first school board election cannot be moved to June, and to check with Senator Sandall on what the draft energy bill would allow cities to build. - The mayor asked staff and council to think about which other annexations the city should pursue so it is not caught flat-footed again; no direction was given on which ones. ## Meeting map | Agenda ref | Topic | ~Start (elapsed) | One-line note | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | State population estimates and redistricting | 0:02 | A bill would build Utah's population counts from the bottom up instead of the top down. | | 1 | Power supply, data centers and city-owned generation | 0:06 | The longest item: three data centers want close to half of Utah's total power. | | 1 | School funding, bonding for the new district, and the school board election | 0:38 | The council wants a June election so the new board can start work sooner. | | 1 | Housing bills, affordable housing money, and a coalition of growing cities | 0:55 | The city is launching a mortgage assistance program and wants allies at the Legislature. | | 1 | State trust land development | 1:20 | Both cities see a coming fight over the state's power to develop land without city input. | | 2.A | Annexation next to Silver Lake — with Saratoga Springs officials | 1:35 | Roads, density and who controls what gets built on 162 acres. | | 2.B | The new high school site — with two school board members | 1:50 | Frank exchange about traffic, safety and how late the cities were brought in. | | 2.C | Legislative priorities list and the strategic plan | 2:45 | Two lists have drifted apart; staff will merge them. | | 2.D | Project management software and city uses for artificial intelligence | 3:05 | Software choice expected by year's end; ideas for loading city code into a chatbot. | | 2.D | Possible citizen and council committees | 3:35 | The mayor and a councilmember each brought a list; roughly twenty ideas surfaced. | | 2.A | Decision on the annexation letter | 4:25 | The council returned to the question and settled it. | | 3 | Adjournment | 4:48 | Closed at about 1:03 p.m. with no motion recorded. | **Discussed but NOT on the agenda:** the city's electricity shortage and whether Eagle Mountain should generate its own power; the timing of the new school district's first board election; the city's new mortgage assistance program; project management software and artificial intelligence tools; and a long brainstorm about creating citizen committees. **On agenda but little/no discussion:** the "other master plans" half of the facilities item — master plans came up only in passing, when the legislative affairs director noted that tracking them falls under his job description. The council also never took a formal motion to adjourn. ## What was discussed ### 1 — Legislative breakfast: counting people and drawing lines Representative Stephanie Gricius opened by describing a bill she is working on with the state's population committee. Utah currently leans on census projections, which she called "very top down," and she wants to flip that so cities feed their own numbers upward. Road money and other state distributions are handed out on population, and she said the state's figure for Eagle Mountain runs roughly 18,000 people below what the city believes is true. She asked the city to cooperate when the population committee calls; staff said a meeting was already being scheduled. A councilmember pressed on whether the same better data could be used to redraw representation more often than once a decade. Gricius said redistricting is set in the state constitution, so changing it would need a ballot question, and the next chance to put one to voters is two years out. She thought the idea might still work at the local level depending on how the language reads, and said legal counsel was looking at it. ### 1 — Legislative breakfast: power, data centers and whether to build our own This was the longest stretch of the morning. Eagle Mountain's data centers need more electricity than the grid can deliver, and two projects have already put on the brakes. The figures given around the table were one project at 800 megawatts, another somewhere between 400 and 700 with room to scale, and a third quoted as "1.4" without a clear unit — together, members said, approaching half of Utah's entire consumption. The lobbyist told the group the state needs roughly the equivalent of Wyoming's total power use, that the governor, Senate president and House speaker had met with Rocky Mountain Power a month earlier, and that new transmission lines cannot be built without pushing consumer rates up sharply. Members asked the obvious question: why not build a plant ourselves? The answer was that state rules would force the city to feed any power it generated back into Rocky Mountain Power's grid rather than keep it. Senator Scott Sandall is drafting a comprehensive energy bill with "triggers" — essentially, either the utility invests or communities get freed to generate their own. The city attorney confirmed later that Eagle Mountain could charge impact fees for electricity, though not for natural gas, and that it was an open question whether that applies to generation alone or requires distribution too. The council talked about small modular nuclear reactors, but was told a nuclear plant is a ten-year project on a fast track, and the shortage is now. Coal and gas came up as the bridge. The lobbyist explained that the Delta plant is converting from coal to gas, that turning coal plants back up runs into federal air rules that cover the whole state rather than any one site, and that the state energy office has only recently been rebuilt under a new director. Members wanted to know who to lobby. The answer was the federal delegation as much as the state: Congressman Curtis had committed before the election to come out and talk, and the mayor said he would push to hold him to it. A councilmember summed up the frustration plainly — waiting five to seven years would simply send the projects to other states, and the problem is not only data centers but the homes, schools and grocery stores coming with the city's growth. ### 1 — Legislative breakfast: schools, taxes and the new district The council asked whether school funding would take another hit. Gricius said the state puts more money into schools every year, and described an unusual shift showing up in the first numbers of the season: income tax down slightly, sales tax up slightly, which reverses the usual pattern of a surplus on the income tax side and a squeezed general fund. Most of the energy went to the new school district split off from Alpine. The district needs new legislation before it can bond, and cannot build a school until that passes — a real problem when members put the timeline to open a school at six years and believe they are already behind. Gricius said support for that bill would not be a problem: "We'll lift the crap out of it." The council's bigger complaint was the election date. The first board election was moved from a June special election to November, and members wanted it moved back so a local board could start making decisions sooner. Gricius and others walked through why that is hard — candidates have to file, ballots have to be printed, and a change would need to pass with an immediate effective date at the very start of the session. She also warned the council that not everyone involved wants June, and agreed to take the question to Senator Brammer. A related thread: the county has to draw board districts, and members were unsure whether that is done by registered voters or by census population, and how often it can be redone. ### 1 — Legislative breakfast: housing bills and a coalition of growing cities The mayor asked to meet with the legislators driving housing policy, saying the bills coming out of the Commission on Housing Affordability land disproportionately on cities like his. He wanted to understand their pressure points and "become a partner rather than a resistant receiver of new law," and to explore tying infrastructure money to the communities actually absorbing the units. He put Eagle Mountain at 1,200 new residential units year to date and Saratoga Springs over 1,400, with 27 percent of them multifamily. Cliff then described the mortgage assistance program the city has just adopted, funded by redevelopment dollars generated by Meta and Tyson — a couple of million dollars already in the account. Most homeownership programs cap out at 80 percent of area median income, where there is little product to buy; Eagle Mountain set its cap at 120 percent, which state law allows for homeownership, with public employees as the primary target. He expects it to start in January and to help roughly twenty to forty households in the first year, and warned the council that the state workforce services department has questioned the 120 percent figure. The blunter part of the conversation was about who actually sets prices. A member argued that stripping zoning from cities does not produce an affordable product: "We do smaller units. We're doing more units per acre. And what do they do? They fill every single one of those with a million-dollar home." Gricius agreed cities get blamed, said she has fought those bills, and pointed to a road-funding bill she helped hold and gut in committee as proof that a couple of votes can matter. The strategy discussed was solidarity: a bloc of cities over 5,000 people signing letters together, a growth caucus forming in the House, and a January meeting in American Fork with the Utah League of Cities and Towns director, with seven cities already committed and hopes of reaching eleven. ### 1 — Legislative breakfast: state trust land Both cities flagged state trust land as the coming statewide fight. The concern is that the agency wants authority to entitle and develop its land with little input from the city that will have to serve it — water, sewer, roads and schools all landing on the municipality after the fact. One participant called it "a battleground. Every city who borders [it]. If we lose, everybody loses." Members compared it to a large unincorporated development in Salt Lake County, and noted that Eagle Mountain's worst road impacts came from trust land, in a way the city still cannot catch up with. The counter-argument offered was that the agency has spent down its credibility at the Legislature, and that leadership is unlikely to hand it the keys. ### 2.A — Annexation discussion with Saratoga Springs The Saratoga Springs mayor and a councilmember came to talk about 162 acres on the shared boundary. No formal annexation petition has been filed yet; what exists is a notice of intent from the church that owns the land, plus one from the school district as applicant, and a request that Eagle Mountain write a letter of support. The land sits next to Saratoga's district area plan, an agreement that gives the church 18,000 units across roughly 3,000 acres. Eagle Mountain members' first worry was density transfer — that the applicant could shift units from elsewhere in that plan onto the new ground and ring the future high school with townhomes. The Saratoga officials said their plan gives them legislative authority over the type and location of what gets built, and that they are not granting additional density. Eagle Mountain members suggested a cleaner approach: annex the land straight into a zone both cities are comfortable with, single-family lots under 6,000 square feet, rather than folding it into the larger plan at all. The sharper worry was roads. Five streets could connect to the parcel — four out of Silver Lake and one out of the Kiowa Valley area — and three of them are residential. One runs past an elementary school on a roundabout; another is a 25 mph street that already carries school traffic past Brookhaven, where roughly 1,200 students walk because there are no buses. Members described traffic backing up from Mountain View Corridor past the shopping center each morning until about 9:30. Adding hundreds of inexperienced teenage drivers to those streets was, as one councilmember put it, "the hill I'm willing to die on." Both councils agreed the more useful outcome of the meeting was simply that they now hold the same position, so the applicant cannot play one city against the other — something both said had happened before on a project at 2100 North. They also spent time on Mid Valley Road, the future connection from Eagle Mountain out to Mountain View Corridor. The two cities' maps do not currently agree on where it lands, and members want that settled before the school design fixes anything in place. The consensus was that it needs to be a fast road with no driveways on it, and that where it meets the corridor should eventually be a free-flowing interchange rather than a signal that would stack traffic back into neighborhoods. ### 2.B — The new high school site and how school locations get chosen Two Alpine School District board members joined by video. Eagle Mountain's objection was that the site sits close to another high school, close to three elementary schools, and at a point where traffic is already the worst in the area. Members asked whether the district would consider a land swap with a property owner farther north; they said the landowner had approached the city, not the other way around, and that the site could be cleared within twelve months. A board member pushed back on the timing. The property has been under contract about a year through four amendments, the current extension runs only to January, roughly $8 million has gone into architecture, soil work has been redone for the current location, and a contractor has already been engaged for that specific site. The school is not yet funded — the district still needs the Legislature to fix the code before it can trigger a lease revenue bond — and she was candid that going back to the board to restart would be difficult: "It's going to be a hard enough of an ask." She also said flatly that she does not like the site either, that traffic and safety problems will exist wherever a school of this size goes, and that the real driver is how many students Utah packs into each building. Washington County builds its high schools for about 1,500 students; this one is designed to open at roughly 2,100. Once a map was finally shared, tempers cooled. The current location had moved south and east, closer to Mountain View Corridor, which several members agreed was "the least of the worst" because most traffic would come off the corridor rather than through neighborhoods. That map was the third version, and the first anyone from either city had seen — a point Eagle Mountain members returned to repeatedly: "we can see this property from Eagle Mountain without binoculars," and the district talked to Saratoga Springs but not to them. The board members apologized, committed to better communication, offered non-disclosure agreements if price sensitivity is the obstacle, and proposed sitting down with each city in March to look at long-range city plans and identify future school sites in advance. The broader conversation was about the fact that cities cannot say no to a school location. Members traded examples — an elementary school built essentially against a highway, a road that was supposed to be a major east-west connection but was killed by school placement, and a case where the district bought the wrong parcel and later needed a swap. Ideas floated included requiring school sites in development agreements, having the city buy land and set the price, and — the suggestion that got the biggest reaction — writing a district policy that requires the board to coordinate with cities on siting. A board member confirmed the new board will be able to write its own policies and said she would want to be part of that. ### 2.C — Legislative priorities list and the strategic plan Cliff handed out the legislative priorities list, and the council's main concern was that it and the strategic plan have drifted apart. As one member put it, "what's the part of a strategic plan if you have competing interests?" The direction was to find the overlap, identify the outliers, and then decide whether an outlier belongs on the plan or does not belong at all. Members also asked for a more usable format: a shortened version with just item titles and a phrase, tabs broken out by department so the council can see that planning is carrying thirty or forty items before piling on more, and a view-only shared document so updates do not have to be emailed. Cliff agreed, and noted the tabs would mean reorganizing how he keeps the master list. The council decided to work through it in chunks at regular meetings rather than in one sitting, starting with the busiest department, and that members should read it individually first so they arrive with opinions. A related thread was capacity. Several members said the point of the exercise is to have an honest conversation when the answer is that a task will bump something else or require outside help. The city is hiring a management policy analyst to support the legislative and strategic planning work. The council also praised the way the last legislative session was tracked, with one member saying advance warning on bills is what lets them make a phone call and say "you need to watch this one." ### 2.D — Project management software and artificial intelligence Staff is demonstrating project management software, narrowed to three to five vendors, at least one of which connects to the financial system the city already uses, with a decision hoped for by year's end. The council's strong recommendation was to buy the training and setup help along with the product, and to hire outside help for the data entry rather than have senior staff spend months typing. As one member put it, the most expensive employees should not be the ones doing data entry, and a scanning company in Eagle Mountain could handle the old paper records. The goal described was an accountability structure where the council can look at a project's status without calling anyone, and the only conversation left is about priority and obstacles. Artificial intelligence came up as a practical tool. Members and staff had returned from a city managers' conference impressed by what other cities are doing — Santa Clara used it to review bills and saved substantial hours, Saratoga Springs uses it on planning documents, and a city in Arizona was cited as going furthest. The concrete suggestion was to load the city's own code into a chatbot so anyone can ask what the setback is for a given yard, with whoever updates the code website also updating the chatbot. Staff reported that about half the department heads already use these tools for document review, and cautioned that answers still have to be checked — though checking is faster than searching. One member suggested bringing in an information technology director who lives in Eagle Mountain to run a staff training on how the technology can be misused; he has demonstrated cloning council members' voices from public recordings to make a fake call to a staff member about a check. ### 2.D — Possible citizen and council committees The mayor walked through a brainstorm list, with the model being two council members of differing perspectives on each committee plus residents and outside experts. His ideas: art; annexations, tied to making the north end an outdoor recreation area and a possible rodeo grounds; power generation; open space, parks and trails; flood control; emergency preparedness, reviving the group that once linked the city with ham radio volunteers and neighborhood teams; a "large lot success" committee to work out why projects like one large-lot subdivision have struggled; venues; historical preservation, including the petroglyphs and local history that could support tourism; and agriculture as a business, asking what farming and cattle can realistically look like here given the soil, water and short season. A councilmember produced a similar list written two years ago: economic development; roads and engineering; parks, open space and cemetery; planning, building and design review, possibly including an architectural review function; neighborhood improvement, beautification and historical preservation; water, storm water and sewer, with a public education component; public safety, military and veterans; community relations, events and recreation; library, public education and elections, which could take on candidate debates and voter information; and legislative and code. Another member added information technology, both for the mutual aid arrangements cities use after a cyberattack and to tap local talent for library programming. Health and wellbeing was added as well. Cliff offered the caution that landed: committees generate work. He described a robust committee system at a previous city that was not a third this long, and warned about both staff time spent attending and the workload created by the ideas that come out. He still recommended them, along with keeping minutes so the rest of the council stays informed. The council agreed it is not comfortable creating all of them, that some should be combined at the start and split later, and that they might be organized under the city's six strategic goals. Annexation and power generation were named the two most important right now. ### 2.A — The decision on the annexation letter Late in the meeting the council came back to whether to send the letter. The city attorney explained why it was requested: a city cannot approve an annexation that leaves an unincorporated island or peninsula unless certain conditions are met, one of which is that the land not sit inside another city's annexation policy plan — unless that city agrees. So Eagle Mountain's letter is the legal key. Members went back and forth on whether withholding it would accomplish anything. The consensus was that it would delay rather than prevent, that the city would be blamed for holding up a high school, and that saying yes to this parcel effectively gives up any claim to the strip running north to south behind it, which the city could not serve or reach anyway. Members also asked whether refusing could protect the neighborhood streets. The attorney's answer was that it could not: if Saratoga Springs decided a road had to connect, it could acquire the right of way through eminent domain even inside Eagle Mountain's boundary. One member argued the city gets more from goodwill and influence with Saratoga's council than from a protest, and another that the road the city badly wants — the connection out to Mountain View Corridor — needs Saratoga's cooperation anyway. The council settled on a letter saying Eagle Mountain does not plan to protest, while stating serious concerns and recording that the city is acting in good faith on Saratoga Springs' assurances that both councils want single-family homes there and will work together on roads and school safety. A member noted that none of it is binding, but "if they back out on it, they back out on it" — at least it will be on paper. ## Notable moments - **"That's the hill I'm willing to die on."** A councilmember said he could accept most compromises but not teenage drivers pouring onto 25 mph residential streets where a thousand-plus children walk to school: "I know all of them. This is my community." - **A board member's apology.** After a tense exchange over the high school, an Alpine board member told the same councilmember she was sorry for "biting your head off," said she does not like the site either, and explained the frustration came from months of fighting over the project rather than from the city's questions. - **The petroglyphs.** Asked why he distrusts assurances about land protection, the mayor described getting a call from the state that petroglyphs at a nearby development were being destroyed. He called the developer, who said he was on it. "They destroyed them all." - **"We're the state, we know what we're doing."** A participant recalled a city inspector telling a school crew they were building on the wrong parcel and being brushed off; the district later had to negotiate a land swap with a bank that owned the property. - **The mayor on the road.** Mayor Gray left partway through and stayed connected by phone, cutting in later to say he was still listening but could barely hear — prompting a scramble to move a microphone. - **"Straw poll, not offline vote."** When the state representative suggested the council could just take a vote by text between meetings, the city attorney corrected the terminology on the spot, to laughter. - **An unplanned salary review.** After a staff member suggested the city could buy land from a developer at a set price and sell it to the school district, a councilmember told him he had "just earned your salary today" — which turned into an extended joke about it being Friday. - **No public comment.** The transcript records no public comment period and no residents addressing the body; this was a working retreat rather than a regular business meeting. ## About this transcript Several proper nouns are mangled by the automatic transcription. The visiting lawmaker is rendered "Representative Grecious" and is Representative Stephanie Gricius, whose first name appears correctly later. "Kimsky Gardner" and "Kim Gardner" refer to the Kem C.
