Gardner Policy Institute; "Scott Sandel" is Senator Scott Sandall; "Camdeal" and "Cam deal" are Cameron Diehl of the Utah League of Cities and Towns; "Mike McFell" and "McKellen" are Senator Mike McKell; "Ray White" is corrected in the room to Stephen Whyte. "IPT" is the Intermountain Power Project in Delta. "Simple land" and "Sittler" are the state trust lands agency. "Steve Monkford" is almost certainly Steve Mumford. School names appear as Brookhaven, Silver Lake, Desert Sky, Blackridge, Westlake and Cedar Valley; "Provolt" and "Provost" are Provo High. The acronyms for the development agreements are unreliable throughout — the same document is called a DAP, MAP, MPA, NBA and MBA within a few lines. One power figure is quoted as "1.4 megawatts," which does not fit the surrounding discussion; the unit is likely wrong. Speaker attribution is limited. There was no roll call, no one is introduced formally, and elected officials from two cities, city staff, a lobbyist and two school board members all speak. Where the recording does not make the speaker clear, this summary says "a councilmember" rather than guessing. One councilmember is addressed only as Donna; her surname is never stated on the recording. The same is true of the school board members Julie and Joylin, the Saratoga Springs councilmember, and the lobbyist, whose name is rendered inconsistently as "Mr. Stewart" and "Mr. Stern." The long stretch spent looking at a shared map is the hardest section to follow: speakers point at a screen and say "this piece," "right here" and "that purple road," so the geography cannot be fully reconstructed from audio alone. There are also several minutes of crosstalk, video-conference troubleshooting and side jokes, and the opening line misstates the date as November 2.

docs.title: City Council Meeting — 2026-08-04 (minutes not yet published)
docs.text: Meeting of 2026-08-04. The minutes for this meeting have not been published yet, so the site has no motion list or roll-call record for it — the account below comes from the meeting recording and its transcript. **In short:** The council spent its afternoon work session on a townhome garage redesign, a statewide healthy-community award application, a satellite company's worry about being built in, and a first look at the city's full project list. In the evening it swore in a new Youth Council, met the 2026 Miss Eagle Mountain royalty, took public comment on a federal grant plan, and approved a Scenic Mountain rezoning and a major update to the city's road plan. **Present:** Mayor Jared Gray; Councilmembers Melissa Clark, Brett Wright, Craig Whiting, Rich Wood, and Zac Huish. All five councilmembers voted on every roll call; no one was recorded as excused or remote. **Staff:** Ben (city manager, consolidated project list), Steve (community services, Healthy Utah application), Brad (public works, water and treatment-plant grades), Brandon (planning, zoning maps and Scenic Mountain rezoning), David Salazar (assistant city engineer, Transportation Master Plan), Evan (administration, flagged the grant agenda error), Marcus (legal advice on motion wording), Lacie Messerly (city recorder), John Magnus (keeper of the legislative priorities list), plus a housing staff member who answered questions on the federal grant plan. Outside presenters: a developer representative for Towns at Brylee Farms, Taylor Keyes (Element Homes), and Corey Wofford (president) and Rusty Layton of LBiSat. ## Decisions | # | Agenda ref | Motion | Moved / Seconded | Vote | Result | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | 4 | Adjourn to a closed session under Section 52-4-205(1) of the Utah Code (6:06 p.m.) | Whiting / Wood | 5-0 (Huish, Wood, Whiting, Wright, Clark all yes) | Passed | | 2 | 8.A | Approve KJ Call as Youth Council Mayor for a term until the next Youth Council election in 2027 | Whiting / Wood | 5-0 (Clark, Wright, Whiting, East 1000 North line and deleting the stale Canyon Wash connection on the wildlife map) | Wright / Wood | 5-0 (Huish, Clark, Wright, Whiting, Wood all yes) | Passed | | 7 | — | Move into a closed session under Section 52-4-205 of the Utah Code | Wood / Whiting | 5-0 (Clark, Wright, Whiting, Wood, Huish all yes) | Passed | | 8 | 20 | Adjourn (9:41 p.m.) | Wood / Wright | Voice vote, unanimous | Passed | **Settled without a vote:** - The council told the Brylee Farms developer it would only entertain shrinking the required 600-square-foot garages if the townhomes around the outside of the project — the ones with no garage requirement at all — get bigger garages in trade, and the developer agreed to check what is still buildable and come back. - The council dropped its request for extra overflow parking at Brylee Farms after hearing the site already provides 386 stalls against a 378-stall requirement and that adding more would mean deleting a home. - The council backed the Healthy Utah Community application — nine strategies the city already does, plus three new ones — and directed staff to have the mayor sign and submit it that night under an extension. - The council took no action on LBiSat's sight-line concerns but asked staff to pass along a contact at the neighboring data center company so the two businesses can work out setbacks directly, and public works agreed to coordinate offline on the treatment plant expansion to the south. - On the citywide project list, the council directed staff to rank projects within each department first, then bring the ranking back for the council to adjust, and asked that man-hours, funding source, and timelines be added. - The council agreed to hold a short virtual special meeting on Monday, August 10 at 3:30 p.m. to act on the federal grant plan, because that item was mistakenly noticed as a hearing only and the plan is due August 14. - Staff was asked to bring back a work session on where additional directional "ladder" signs are needed, supported by a heat map from the chamber, and a separate work session on stacked recreational-vehicle trailer parking on half-acre to one-acre lots. - The council agreed the landscaped medians on Ranches Parkway will come out, and that a full landscape design for the road shoulders will come back to the council before construction. - Staff agreed to help Cedar Valley High School put together a simplified application so its proposed family community center can be considered for federal grant money. ## Meeting map | Agenda ref | Topic | ~Start (elapsed) | One-line note | designation | 0:25 | Nine existing strategies and three new ones endorsed; application submitted that night. | | 1.C | LBiSat property — clear lines of sight | 0:50 | Satellite firm asked for protection from tall neighbors; council pointed to private negotiation. | | 1.D | Consolidated project list | 1:15 | City manager walked through roughly 400 projects and asked how to rank them. | | 3 | Agenda review | 1:50 | Consent items cleared; the federal grant item's noticing error surfaced. | | 17 | Legislative priorities | 1:55 | Water and housing lead at the state level; sign and trailer Information items and upcoming events | 3:07 | Youth Council Summer Splash, Truth in Taxation hearing, farmers market, Ties and Tiaras. | | 8.A | Youth Council appointments | 3:10 | A mayor and seventeen members sworn in. | | 9.A | Miss Eagle Mountain royalty introduction | 3:14 | Three young women introduced their service projects. | | 10 | Public comments | 3:16 | One speaker on the proposed property tax increase. | | 11 | Council and mayor items | 3:19 | Every member responded to the tax comment and praised the youth. | | 12–14 | Consent agenda | 3:30 | Approved without discussion. | | 15.A | Federal grant annual action plan hearing | 3:36 | One comment; action pushed to a special meeting. | | 16.A | Scenic Mountain rezoning | 3:45 | Housekeeping rezone of about 200 parcels off expired zones. | | 16.B | Transportation Master Plan and impact fee plan | 3:55 | The night's longest item; medians, Ranches Parkway, and school access dominated. | | 18 | Liaison reports | 4:50 | Transit, Youth Council, community services, and fire district updates. | | 20 | Adjournment | 5:41 | Adjourned at 9:41 p.m. after a second closed session. | **Discussed but NOT on the agenda:** the proposed property tax increase and Thursday's Truth in Taxation hearing, additional builder directional signs on the south end of the city, stacked trailer and recreational-vehicle parking on mid-size lots, a proposed family community center at Cedar Valley High School, a transit on-demand ride service open house, and the scheduling of a special meeting for August 10. **On agenda but little/no discussion:** the July 21 minutes, the chapel and recreation building site plan, and the related development agreement ordinance all passed on the consent agenda without comment; the city manager information items were folded into the project list presentation; and the financial report and upcoming agenda items were not taken up. ## What was discussed ### 1.A — Towns at Brylee Farms Phase B update The developer of this townhome project returned to show design changes the council asked for at an earlier meeting. Under the existing development agreement, forty of the townhomes must be three stories with a garage of at least 600 square feet. Only twenty have been built, and the developer said buyers keep choosing the two-story plan instead. The proposal is to build twenty-one two-story units with a garage pushed out about three feet — 24 feet deep and 496 square feet — plus a 520-square-foot unfinished basement the three-story slab-on-grade plan does not have. Councilmember Wright said swapping a 600-square-foot garage for a 496-square-foot one, on its own, is a downside with no upside for residents. He asked whether the smaller standard garages elsewhere in the project could be enlarged in exchange. Councilmember Wood pressed on width instead of depth: the garage is 20.08 feet wide either way, because the lots are platted and the utilities are already stubbed, and he worried about two cars and people trying to get out of them in bad weather. Councilmember Clark floated extra overflow parking, possibly by deleting a lot. Staff and the developer said the parking count already exceeds the requirement, and Wood agreed more stalls were not realistic. The council landed on a single ask: come back with bigger garages on the outer-perimeter buildings that have not been poured yet, and then the amendment to the development agreement would likely find support. The developer also agreed to switch from a lot line adjustment to a full plat amendment because city staff find it easier to administer, which Wright thanked them for. ### 1.B — Healthy Utah Community designation A statewide nonprofit offers a Healthy Utah Community designation to cities that can show they have already put nine health strategies in place across three areas — active living, access to healthy food, and mental health — and commit to three more over the next three years. The city passed a resolution to pursue this a year ago but lacked a health coalition; the new Community Services Board now fills that role, and a deadline extension left one day to submit. Staff walked through the nine strategies the board recommended: the Thanksgiving Turkey Trot, the recently approved off-street trails master plan, safe routes to schools work, the library seed exchange, the library emergency food pantry, a farmers market that accepts federal food benefits, the Believer City designation and Motivational Mile, senior citizen programming, and free gun locks at the library. Staff also shared county-level health data showing the city above the state average on high blood pressure, obesity, and adults reporting fair or poor health. For the three new commitments, the board suggested a campaign to destigmatize mental illness, trail wayfinding signs that show time and distance, and adaptive recreation programs so residents with disabilities do not have to drive to other cities to participate. Every councilmember voiced support. Wright asked that a resident trying to start a Special Olympics chapter be brought into the effort, and Wood pushed for community gardens in several locations, including possibly on weedy undeveloped open space. Public works noted an earlier garden site near Pioneer Park already has water but failed after three seasons. ### 1.C — LBiSat property, maintaining clear lines of sight LBiSat is a satellite communications hosting company that moved to Eagle Mountain from South Jordan and built on ten acres off Pony Express. Its business depends on a clear, roughly 10-degree view to the horizon in all directions for its dishes. Company representatives said they chose the site partly because the surrounding land was light industrial, with height limits they could live with, and they are alarmed that nearby parcels now appear to allow taller buildings. Their contracts, they said, are multimillion-dollar and will go elsewhere if the sight lines are lost. Councilmember Huish framed the core tension as property rights — the council would be restricting what neighbors can build, and he was not sure the city can zone airspace. Wright compared it to homeowners who assume a view is permanent and said the honest answer is probably that the city cannot and should not restrict neighbors; he offered instead to consider height exceptions so LBiSat could raise its own antennas. Wood asked bluntly why the company bought ten acres rather than enough land to protect itself, and suggested buying the setback it needs. Planning staff then delivered mostly reassuring news: the neighboring data center's plan puts a retention basin 320 feet from the shared line, the buildings across the street top out near 24 feet, and the city's own treatment plant sits on ground about 10 to 15 feet lower with no plans above two stories. Public works cautioned that a 250-foot buffer would consume the plant's entire buildable footprint, and LBiSat's engineer said that number was conservative and likely shrinks to about 210 feet or less. Staff offered to connect the company with a contact at the data center. ### 1.D — Consolidated project list The city manager presented a first consolidated list of everything the city has underway — capital projects, non-capital projects, initiatives, and hard one-off tasks — separate from day-to-day operations and emergency response. He framed it with the city's priority order: public safety as the foundation, then essential infrastructure, then economic prosperity, then quality of life. His repeated line was that the staff can do anything but not everything, and that spreading thin is how organizations fail. The tour covered transportation projects such as school-area pedestrian safety work, free right turns at Silver Lake and Woodhaven, median removal on Ranches Parkway, and widening Pony Express south of Eagle Mountain Boulevard, which a data center company is funding directly. On water and sewer it included several wells in various stages, new booster stations, a six-million-gallon-per-day treatment plant expansion now going through bonding and permitting, and a reuse permit. Parks, facilities, a possible shift in how fire service is funded, and a possible change in how law enforcement is provided were all on the list. Asked how to prioritize, he recommended that department staff rank their own projects first, then hand the list to the council to adjust and finalize. Whiting and Huish agreed staff are closest to the work. Clark asked that the list flag anything at a critical state, such as treatment capacity, so choices are informed rather than arbitrary. Wood asked for man-hours, cost, and funding source on each line, arguing that seeing how many projects sit on one person explains why some never finish. Wright said some items should simply be deleted, naming an ice skating rink; the mayor explained that one only lives on if outside donations cover it. ### 15.A — Federal grant annual action plan public hearing The Community Development Block Grant program sends federal money through the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development for community development work, and the city must adopt and submit an annual plan describing how it will spend its share after holding two public hearings. The first was in April; this was the second. Staff had discovered in the work session that the item was noticed as a hearing only, with no action attached, and the plan is due August 14 — before the next regular meeting. Hence the special meeting set for August 10. One resident spoke. Charlotte Dukos described a new family-focused community center that Cedar Valley High School plans to create by converting part of a portable building, with showers, pantry items, and adult education, open to the wider community beyond school hours. She asked that capital money from the grant be considered for it. Staff said it could plausibly qualify as a public facility and offered a simplified application to test eligibility. Clark asked whether donated labor from local builders would jeopardize the funding; staff said no, as long as the contractors are qualified, and that it would stretch the money. Wright walked through the funding buckets he saw — roughly $181,000 for public facilities and infrastructure, $200,000 for affordable housing, and $36,900 for public services — and asked how the specific projects inside each bucket get decided. Staff said individual agreements would come back to the council for approval, and that small shifts between buckets are allowed while larger ones require a plan amendment. ### 16.A — Ordinance rezoning certain lands known as Scenic Mountain This was cleanup. Planning is working through the zoning map to find areas still carrying zones that no longer exist in the city code, and replacing them with current equivalents. About two hundred parcels in the Scenic Mountain area carry old designations from an expired agreement, which means staff has to dig through archived code versions just to answer a resident asking how far from the line they can put a shed. The item also amends the general plan's future land use map, which currently shows commercial on land that turned out to be state transportation right-of-way. The Planning Commission and staff both recommended approval, and no one spoke at the public hearing. The debate was entirely about how to word the motion. Wright pointed out that the zoning change was spelled out clearly but the general plan change was not, and legal counsel said a general plan amendment would normally be its own agenda item with its own motion. Since it was noticed as one item, counsel said one motion was acceptable this time. Whiting's original motion referenced the chart of affected properties; Wright offered substitute language naming both the general plan amendment and the rezoning map, Whiting adopted it, and Wood kept his second. ### 16.B — Ordinance amending the Transportation Master Plan and Impact Fee Facilities Plan The assistant city engineer brought back the road plan and the impact fee plan, updated after an unusually busy year. The changes include a new priority project list, a new name and classification for the east-west highway formerly called Mid Valley Road, a new principal arterial classification to clear up confusion between five- and seven-lane roads, refreshed traffic modeling, and updated costs so the transportation impact fee is accurate. Staff also stopped assuming outside money from the regional planning organization and developers, which had been baked into the old cost figures. Two changes drew most of the discussion. The first was Silver Lake Parkway, where a study recommends replacing a roundabout at Golden Eagle with a traffic signal, pulling the school crossings down to that controlled intersection, and squaring up a skewed leg. Staff explained the trail would be realigned but its distance from pavement kept, and a new shoulder would push traffic farther from walkers. A second signal is proposed at Woodhaven. Three residents spoke in favor, including a school principal who said local high schools average roughly 900 students per access point and the connection matters for getting students in and out safely. The second was Ranches Parkway, where the plan removes the wide landscaped medians and adds a travel lane each direction plus a center turn lane, with two new signals and restricted turns elsewhere. Huish pushed to keep some median for the sake of the city's character at its entrance. Wright disagreed, citing maintenance crews being struck, water soaking into the roadbed, and the volume of traffic the corridor now carries. Wood took a middle position: take the medians out, but make the roadside landscaping as striking as what is lost. Whiting agreed and asked for a landscape architect. Staff said design money is already inside the roughly $11.8 million project, which is expected to be awarded regional funding the following Thursday, and that a plan will come back to the council. ## Notable moments - **A resident called the proposed tax increase a bait and switch.** Duncan "DJ" Searcy told the council that a 220% increase is a real burden on neighbors living paycheck to paycheck and on retirees who moved to the city for low property taxes, and that framing the increase around law enforcement while it also funds capital projects "rubbed people the wrong way." - **Every councilmember answered him directly.** Wood said "I don't think that you're totally wrong" and promised clearer information at Thursday's hearing. Whiting said the mayor had warned the next four years would be the toughest because data center revenue has not matured. Clark quoted Spider-Man — "with great power comes great responsibility" — and called the power to tax one of the greatest a person can hold. Huish said he spent his weekend rebuilding every budget figure into a spreadsheet. - **A business owner made a pointed comparison.** LBiSat's president told the council that after listening to a long debate about the size of a townhome garage, "if you can be concerned about the size of a garage, you could be concerned about our look angles." - **A father described near-misses at a school roundabout.** Ben Perez said his son refused to be picked up in front of Silver Lake Elementary and instead crossed at the roundabout, where Perez watched "countless kids" nearly get hit, and said a signal there matters most for children walking home alone. - **The council pushed back on school siting.** Wood told the school district's representative that the new high school "was in the wrong place for every reason" and that everyone is now scrambling to build safe walking and driving routes after the land was already bought. Staff said a recurring meeting with the district is being scheduled. - **A scheduling error forced a special meeting.** Staff realized mid-work-session that the federal grant item had been noticed as a hearing only, with no action possible, and the council spent several minutes trading availability before landing on Monday, August 10 at 3:30 p.m., virtual. - **The new Miss Eagle Mountain chose voter turnout as her cause.** Treea Smith, crowned on her fifth attempt, said turnout in the city is "severely low" and her project is to help young adults register and understand how candidates get on a ballot. - **A transit note with a challenge attached.** Clark promoted an open house for a new on-demand ride service priced at $2.50, saying she wants it wildly successful so she can tell the transit authority "I told you so" and win more routes. ## About this transcript The automatic transcription garbles several proper nouns. Councilmember Zac Huish appears as "Hewish," "Herwish," and "Hughes"; Brett Wright appears once as "Wrobel-Wright." The Brylee Farms project is written "Briley Farms." LBiSat appears as "LVISAT," and Rusty Layton is once rendered "Rusty Lake." Charlotte Dukos's surname is spelled two ways. The park hosting the farmers market and the Youth Council event is variously "Quarry Ride," "Glory Ride," "Cory Wright," and "Corey Ride" — almost certainly one park. The grant program is flipped to "CBDG" in places, the regional planning organization "MAG" is once "MEG," state trust lands appear as "CITLA," and the high-T intersection design is written "high tee." Two numbers conflict: the Ranches Parkway project is cited as both $11.8 million and $11.4 million, and the new high school's opening is stated as "fall of 2024," which does not fit the surrounding discussion. Speaker labels are consistent per voice but not mapped to names, and several labels blur together in fast exchanges — one label carries both Councilmember Wright's remarks and lines clearly spoken by staff or by the visiting royalty. Where the transcript did not make the speaker plain, discussion is attributed generically rather than to a named member. Staff first names are usually clear but surnames rarely are: the city manager is called "Ben" throughout and addressed once as "Mr. Reeves," and the presenters named Steve, Brad, Brandon, Evan, and Marcus are never given surnames. The developer's representative on the first item is never identified by name on the record. A short stretch during the LBiSat slides is hard to follow because microphones were off and speakers were pointing at a screen, and the closed sessions were not recorded.

docs.title: City Council Meeting — 2026-08-06 (minutes not yet published)
docs.text: Meeting of 2026-08-06. The minutes for this meeting have not been published yet, so the site has no motion list or roll-call record for it — the account below comes from the meeting recording and its transcript. **In short:** Eagle Mountain's council held a special evening hearing on a proposed property tax increase and then voted on it the same night. A packed room and a full Zoom line produced nearly three hours of comment, almost all of it against the advertised 220% increase in the city's share of the property tax. Afterward the council talked the rate down and voted 5-0 to raise it by 183% instead — about $250 a year on an average home. **Present:** Mayor Jared Gray (participating remotely by video, citing a previous obligation); Councilmembers Melissa Clark, Brett Wright, Craig Whiting, Rich Wood and Zac Huish, all in the chambers. No member was recorded as excused. **Staff:** Lacie "Lacey" Messerly (city recorder, who ran the speaker list and read written comments), Ben Reeves (city manager), Kimberly (finance staff, who supplied the tax rate and revenue figures), Marcus (legal counsel), Stephanie (recorder's office), Natalie (distributed public packets), Carson (meeting technology), and Sheriff Smith of the Utah County Sheriff's Office, who spoke from the audience at the mayor's invitation. ## Decisions | # | Agenda ref | Motion | Moved / Seconded | Vote | Result | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | 4.A | Approve and adopt a property tax rate of 0.001500 for fiscal year 2026–2027, above the certified rate of 0.000530, increasing the city's budgeted property tax revenue by about $5,591,594, or 183.02% over the prior year exclusive of new growth | Whiting / Wright | 5-0 (roll call: Wood yes, Whiting yes, Wright yes, Clark yes, Huish yes) | Passed | | 2 | 5 | Adjourn | Wood / Wright | Voice vote | Passed | **Settled without a vote:** - The council agreed to bring back an ordinance at a future meeting requiring every future council to review the city's property tax rate each year as part of the budget, after legal counsel confirmed that a council can put such a review in city code even though a later council could change it. - The council agreed to bring back a separate resolution creating a dedicated public safety fund, after finance staff explained that property tax revenue must first be received into the general fund and then moved by operating transfer; the mayor said both items should be addressed at the next council meeting. - The council accepted that a temporary increase is not an option, saying state law does not allow a city to raise a rate for a year or two and then roll it back automatically. - No decision was made about which projects or positions the freed-up sales tax money will actually pay for; the recorder noted that the public hearing on the budget itself is set for August 18. ## Meeting map | Agenda ref | Topic | ~Start (elapsed) | One-line note | |---|---|---|---| | 1, 2 | Call to order, prayer, Pledge of Allegiance | ~0:02 | Wright offered a prayer, Whiting led the pledge, and the mayor joined by video. | | 3.A | Hearing ground rules and packet materials | ~0:04 | Three minutes each, no clapping or booing; in-person speakers first, then online, then email. | | 3.A | Public hearing on the proposed property tax increase | ~0:07 | Roughly 60 people spoke over nearly three hours; the hearing closed at 9:00 p.m. | | 3.A | Reading of the property tax impact schedule | ~3:00 | The mayor read the advertised rate, revenue and household impact figures into the record. | | 3.A | Council, city manager and sheriff respond | ~3:05 | Each member answered themes from the hearing; Reeves and Sheriff Smith also spoke. | | 3.A | Mayor's data center revenue figures | ~3:35 | Gray reported projected QTS tax revenue and a $5 million road commitment. | | 4.A | Resolution setting the property tax rate | ~3:50 | Council talked the rate down from 0.0017 to 0.0015 and adopted it 5-0. | | 5 | Adjournment | ~4:38 | Adjourned at 10:38 p.m. | **Discussed but NOT on the agenda:** starting a city-run police department instead of contracting with the county; the tax impact expected next year from the new Lake Mountain School District; data center tax incentives and the municipal energy tax; the widening of Pony Express Parkway; the city's down payment assistance program; a proposed annual rate-review ordinance and a separate public safety fund; road safety measures near schools; sewer and water capacity. **On agenda but little/no discussion:** nothing was skipped — the call to order, the pledge and the adjournment were routine, and both substantive items were taken up in full. ## What was discussed ### 3.A — Public hearing: the proposal and the objections Utah's Truth in Taxation law requires a city to hold a public hearing before charging more than the "certified" property tax rate — the rate that would bring in roughly the same money as last year. Eagle Mountain advertised a rate of 0.001700 against a certified rate of 0.000530. As the mayor read into the record, that would have raised an extra $6,742,938, a 220.88% increase in the city's own property tax revenue, adding about $314 a year on a home worth $488,000 and about $2,988 on an average business property. The affected budget line was the sheriff's contract, rising by about $1.5 million. That gap between $1.5 million and $6.7 million drove most of the anger. Speaker after speaker said the city had promised that every dollar would go to public safety and only admitted otherwise once residents did the arithmetic. "Eagle Mountain City is proposing a property tax increase with every dollar going straight to public safety, period. So that's a lie, and we all know that now," Duncan Searcy said. Nathan Thornburg put it as a trust problem: "You were either dishonest then or you're dishonest now." Former councilmember Adam Bradley, in a statement read by his wife Melissa Bradley, wrote, "This was never just about public safety." The second theme was cost of living. Bruno Hunsaker spoke for neighbors on Social Security. Mark Cookston said a $27-a-month Social Security raise was already wiped out by a $250 county tax increase last year. Cheryl Carr, 71, said she and her husband would have to sell and move. Shawna Clark said she earns $16 an hour and has a daughter and four grandchildren living with her. Denver Dorrell described a daughter with repeated Life Flight trips and a son whose bleeding was stopped by a deputy — and said the increase would still break his single-income household. ### 3.A — Public hearing: alternatives residents offered, and the voices in favor Residents did not just object; many proposed other places to look. Several pointed to impact fees on new construction, including Dave Bresheenahan, who said he helped write impact fee law as a legislator. Steve Campbell asked whether the city had pursued federal grants. Many asked for a phased increase instead of one jump — Michael Carey proposed a three-to-five-year plan with published outcome measures, and Joel Anderson worked out an alternative that would add three deputies rather than seven and land near an 8% increase. Alex Washburn, online, said he supported raising about $1.5 million to cover the 2027 sheriff's contract and nothing beyond it without a clear list of what the rest funds. Data centers came up repeatedly. Joy Rasmussen and others cited large property tax incentives given to Meta and later projects and argued the city had traded away revenue it now wants from homeowners. Megan Streeter said the city should "stop acting like we need the data centers and start acting like they need us." Zeke Magdaleno and Michael Valentini, who both work on the sites, described the scale of construction underway. Anthony Wood argued the city should look at Eagle Mountain's low crime rate rather than officers-per-thousand comparisons, and raised the roughly $1.13 million the city lost to a scammer in 2022. A handful spoke in favor. Matt Everett called 220% "a direct reflection of poor management and leadership" over 15-plus years but urged the council to pass it anyway. Jeff Ruth described calling for a deputy and being told only two were on duty. Charlotte Dukos, who attends most meetings, said the line-item budget is already online in a 200-page document and that the city has run lean for years — while also urging a smaller, phased number. Tony Castillo, a roofing contractor, backed an increase while saying 220% was shocking. Mark McConkey used his time to ask for something else entirely: a cost study for a city police department, arguing Eagle Mountain is the largest city in Utah without one. ### 3.A — Public hearing: how the council, city manager and sheriff answered After closing the hearing at 9:00 p.m., the mayor gave each member time to respond. Huish opened with an apology on communication — "we failed you" — and said he had produced a podcast at his own expense to add context. Wood was blunter still about the past: "I think we're here because of your irresponsibility. You left this big pile for us," he said of earlier councils that did not raise water, sewer or property rates. Whiting told residents skepticism of government is healthy and asked them to stay for the explanation. Wright said the easy path would have been to do nothing and keep cutting services, and disclosed he is in his fifth year and will not run again. Clark said she had spent weeks looking for savings and that the real question was what to cut. Huish also explained why the "100% public safety" message had been so narrow: the application filed with the state was built around covering the sheriff's contract entirely with property tax, and departing from that application would have disrupted the process. He then listed what the freed-up money had been contemplated for in budget sessions — about $525,000 to bring staff to 90% of median pay, and roughly 18 full- and part-time positions, 13 of them tied to parks, open space and trails, plus a streets operator and several engineering and operations roles. City Manager Ben Reeves said city staff is about a third the size of comparable cities' and that crews have been working "with basically an arm tied behind their back." Sheriff Smith said the deputies assigned here are among his best, that they run call to call, and, "we're not asking for anything that's not needed out here. It is definitely needed. Actually, more is needed." The mayor closed the segment with figures he said came from QTS: the buildings under construction and planned would generate more than $19 million a year across local taxing entities, including about $2.7 million to the city at the current rate and $10.4 million to the new Lake Mountain School District. He added that QTS declined incentives on its next two buildings and, after one phone call, agreed to pay the full roughly $5 million cost of widening Pony Express Parkway. ### 4.A — Resolution: setting the rate at 0.0015 The resolution was the actual decision: whether to adopt a rate above the certified rate for fiscal year 2026–2027. Clark opened by pointing out the line-item budget already exists online for this year and prior years, and the mayor drew a distinction the council returned to all night — that everything had been done in open meetings, so the failure was communication rather than transparency. Whiting then made the case that the "100% to public safety" statement was literally true but badly explained: property tax would become the pillar holding up public safety, freeing the sales tax now propping it up for other work — school-zone speed tables at $70,000 to $80,000 each, a speed study already underway, and road capacity. He added that the city charges the maximum impact fees state law allows and cannot tax data centers at a separate rate. Wood said his reason for supporting a rate at all was stability: sales tax collapses in a downturn, and the need for police does not. He said the city has never had a five-, ten- or twenty-year financial plan, and put the master transportation plan's cost at $419 million by 2035 for Eagle Mountain's share alone. Clark named her top three capital priorities as safe roads to schools, expanding a sewer treatment plant already at capacity for load, and water infrastructure — noting the city asked residents, schools, churches and businesses not to water over the Fourth of July week, and that tanks must stay full to fight wildfires. Huish then argued the advertised number was too high. Benchmarking against Saratoga Springs and the county, he said he could not support 0.0017 and floated 0.0011 as a bare minimum, noting the city is currently the second-lowest rate in Utah County. Others converged toward the middle; Whiting, who had written to a resident weeks earlier that he expected to end below 220%, said he had been looking at about 0.0015. Kimberly ran the numbers: $5,591,594 in new revenue, a 183.02% increase, which Huish described as roughly 70 cents a day for an average household. Whiting moved that rate, Wright seconded, and it passed 5-0 on a roll call. ## Notable moments - **Applause got a warning.** After the first speaker finished, the room clapped; a councilmember reminded people the mayor's rules barred it and said further outbursts would mean being asked to leave. Duncan Searcy answered from the podium a few speakers later: "I don't think our First Amendment rights care much about his decorum." - **A former councilmember spoke through his wife.** Melissa Bradley gave her own comment, then returned to read Adam Bradley's statement. When she tried to add a personal note at the end, she was told she did not get to speak twice. - **A records request became part of the debate.** Joy Rasmussen said Alex Washburn's public records request had been denied and priced beyond what he could pay. Washburn, speaking online, said an hour-long meeting the previous day with Mayor Gray, the city manager, Councilmember Clark and finance staff "genuinely changed my understanding of several things" — and he still asked why fully funding the sheriff through property tax was the right policy. - **One resident changed his mind on the record.** Jacob Moore said he had strongly opposed the increase until he understood how Utah's revenue-driven system works and that the 221% applies only to the city's slice — about 12% of a typical total tax bill. He still asked for a smaller number. - **The sheriff defended deputies taking breaks in public.** Responding to comments about seeing patrol cars at convenience stores, Sheriff Smith said he would rather deputies spend downtime out in the community than back at the office. - **A Civil War analogy closed the case for the increase.** Whiting recounted the defense of Little Round Top at Gettysburg and the bayonet charge, then said: "Sometimes leadership requires leading people to a place they do not want to go because we see a vision that we know we must obtain." - **Councilmembers were told, repeatedly, they would be voted out.** Tracy Perretta said she would spend her time getting Clark and the mayor out of office. Daniel Lob said passage would be "a death knell." An email from Ethan Neal, read into the record, said he would make it his mission to publicize how each member voted. - **The state legislature loomed over the timing.** Several speakers, including Chris Waldron and Kristen Meyer, said raising taxes now because the state might cap increases later is not an ethical reason. Councilmembers confirmed a cap bill was floated and defeated and said they expect it back, along with an effort to spread the municipal energy tax from data centers across other cities. - **Wright announced he is leaving.** "I've started into my second term. This is my fifth year. I'm not going to rerun," he said, framing his vote as free of re-election calculation. - **The mayor's absence was itself a comment.** Mark Espinoza told the council, "I wish he was in front of us looking at all these people here," while several others thanked the city for keeping the remote option open. ## About this transcript The recording was made from speech-to-text, so proper nouns are the least reliable part. Councilmember Zac Huish appears throughout as "Hewish" or "Dewish"; City Recorder Lacie Messerly appears as "Lacey." Resident names were read aloud from sign-in forms and are approximations: "Shedrick D. Shermond" was corrected on the record to Cedric DeChermond, "Joseph Pill—" to Joseph Pedlow, and "Daniel Lamb" to Daniel Lob. "Dave Bresheenahan," "Tracy Perretta" and "Steve Pereda" (who identified each other as spouses), "Charlotte Dukos"/"Duco," and "Zeke Magdalio"/Magdaleno are all rendered inconsistently. Place names suffer too: "Lehigh" is Lehi, and "Corey Ride," "Quarry Ride" and "Cory Bee Ride" all appear to be Cory Wride Memorial Park. Attribution during the public comment period is solid, because the recorder called each name before the person spoke. Attribution during council deliberation is less certain: the mayor called on members by name at the start of the responses, and members addressed each other by first name, which is how the speakers here were identified. Where a voice could not be tied to a specific member — including the councilmember who enforced the no-clapping rule — this summary says "a councilmember." Two staff members, "Kimberly" and "Marcus," were referred to only by first name; their roles are inferred from what they were asked to answer. A few numbers were garbled mid-sentence and have been reported as read: the sheriff's contract budget change was stated as "$1,507,000. $939," and speakers alternated between 220% and 221% or 210% for the advertised increase. The mayor also misspoke the time twice near the opening and corrected himself. Some late-arriving emails were summarized rather than read in full, and one written comment was declared inappropriate and not read aloud.

docs.title: Primary results certified; November ballot set
docs.text: Primary results certified; November ballot set The city certified the August 12 primary, in which 6,866 of 26,930 mailed ballots came back, and named the six candidates advancing to the November 4 election. Nothing changes day to day — this makes the primary official. Your November 4 ballot will list Melissa Clark and Jared Gray for mayor, and Emily Buss, Brett Wright, Craig Whiting, and Charlotte Ducos for council. routine A Resolution of the Board of Canvassers Certifying the Official Canvassers' Report of the August 12, 2025 Municipal Primary Election for Eagle Mountain City, Utah City Recorder Gina Olsen presented the results of the 2025 Municipal Primary Election. The Utah County Elections Office has verified the ballots from the Primary Election with the following results:  26,930 ballots were mailed and a total of 6,866 were returned for a 25.5% return rate.  23 provisional ballots were issued, of which 2 were not counted due to incomplete information on the provisional ballot form.  124 ballots were returned but not counted due to missing signatures (3), signature discrepancies (3), or returned past postmark deadline (116), other reasons (2).  310 residents voted in person on Election Day (or an early vote center).  5 UOCAVA ballots were issued and returned through Enhanced Voting. Councilmember Gray moved that the Board of Canvassers verify the results of the 2025 Municipal Primary Election by ratifying the results of the canvass; accept the report of the Election Official and certify the election results; and declare Four-year Mayoral candidates Melissa Clark and Jared R. Gray; and Four-year City Council candidates Emily Buss, Brett L Wright, Craig Whiting, and Charlotte Ducos eligible to be on the ballot and nominated for the General Municipal Election on November 4, 2025. Councilmember Wood seconded the motion. Outcome: passed with a unanimous vote.. Vote: 5 yes, 0 no. In favor: Brett Wright, Donna Burnham, Jared Gray, Melissa Clark, Rich Wood.

If it passes, you would pay an extra 10 cents on every $100 spent in the city, with the money going to recreation and cultural facilities. notable A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Providing for a Referendum to be held on November 4, 2025, for the purpose of submitting to the qualified voters of Eagle Mountain City, Utah County, Utah the question of authorization of the imposition a 0.1% sales and use tax (one-tenth of one percent) for the purpose of funding recreational, cultural, botanical, and zoological facilities, and botanical, cultural, and zoological organizations within the City (RAP Tax) Councilmember Wright moved to adopt a Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Providing for a Referendum to be held on November 4, 2025, for the purpose of submitting to the qualified voters of Eagle Mountain City, Utah County, Utah the question of authorization of the imposition a 0.1% sales and use tax (one-tenth of one percent) for the purpose of funding recreational, cultural, botanical, and zoological facilities, and botanical, cultural, and zoological organizations within the City (RAP Tax). Councilmember Gray seconded the motion. Outcome: passed with a unanimous vote.. Vote: 5 yes, 0 no. In favor: Brett Wright, Donna Burnham, Jared Gray, Melissa Clark, Rich Wood.

docs.title: City to sell a small parcel to adjoining owners
docs.text: City to sell a small parcel to adjoining owners The city approved selling 0.156 acres of city-owned land to the owners of the neighboring lots, with the sale to be finished by February 19, 2026. Only the owners of the adjoining lots are affected. They can buy the parcels together on one application, and within six months their fences must sit on the correct lot line or be removed. notable A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Approving the Disposal of 0.156 Acres of Designated "Significant Real Property" (Utah County Parcel #49:601:0080) Pursuant to EMMC 3.30.060 and 3.30.070, and Establishing Terms of the Disposal Councilmember Gray moved to adopt a Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Approving the Disposal of 0.156 Acres of Designated "Significant Real Property" (Utah County Parcel #49:601:0080) Pursuant to EMMC 3.30.060 and 3.30.070, and Establishing Terms of the Disposal with terms below: • Approving option two with each landowner of the parcels listed signing the land disposal application. The applicants may combine the application into one land disposal application and fee. • If any landowner, in any of the lots are unwilling or unable to purchase the corresponding parcels, the approval will revert to option one. • It is required that all fences are on the correct lot line or the lots are to have no fence within 6 months of recordation. • The water requirements for each parcel are fulfilled with the purchase of the parcels as deemed appropriate by staff. • The full land disposal application and process must be finalized in six months (February 19, 2026). Councilmember Wood seconded the motion. Outcome: passed with a unanimous vote.. Vote: 5 yes, 0 no. In favor: Brett Wright, Donna Burnham, Jared Gray, Melissa Clark, Rich Wood. Topics: Public Works & Infrastructure.

docs.text: Open space plan adopted, backyard trail dropped The council adopted the city's natural open space and wildlife habitat plan, but cut a walking path planned behind homes between Autumn Lane and East Harvest Lane. The plan also drops its semi-truck parking language and lets goat grazing run as needed rather than on a fixed schedule. notable An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, adopting the Natural Open Space and Wildlife Habitat Management Plan subject to: 1. Councilmember Wright seconded the motion. Discussion took place on the removal of the pedestrian path, its implications for Open Space, and future management of the area confirming that the space will continue to stay classified as Open Space. They also considered options for semi-truck parking, including a designated parking lot. AMENDED MOTION: Councilmember Wood moved to adopt an Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, adopting the Natural Open Space and Wildlife Habitat Management Plan: 1. Removing from the Plan the pedestrian path that goes west from the Walmart property and southwest to Autumn Lane, behind resident backyards between Autumn Lane and East Harvest Lane then ends at Shiloh Way; and 2. Removing the language concerning semi-truck parking; and 3. Amending the grazing period of goats from “two to seven days” to as needed. Councilmember Wright seconded the motion. EMMC 17.25.020(E)(2)(a)(i) and 17.25.020(F)(1)(a)(i) are changed to, “Required Amount of Moderate Income Housing: A minimum of 10% of new residential development in this zone shall be dedicated to moderate income housing (MIH) units priced for occupancy by households with a gross income equal to or less than 80% of the median gross income for Utah County per Utah Code 10-9a-103.” Councilmember Gray seconded the motion Councilmember Wright moved to approve an Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Amending the Eagle Mountain Municipal Code Chapter 17.25 Residential Zones with the following changes: 1. docs.title: Bigger no-build buffer around natural washes
docs.text: Bigger no-build buffer around natural washes The council took up a rule barring permanent buildings and earthwork within 75 feet of a wash's center flowline, or 50 feet from its bank, whichever is greater. If your lot backs onto a dry wash, this limits how close you can build or dig. It applies to homes, shops, and business parks alike, with the city engineer measuring the buffer. notable An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Amending the Eagle Mountain Municipal Code Chapters 17.25 Residential Zones, 17.35 Commercial Zones, and 17.37 Business Park Zones with the following change: 1. The amendment in 17.25.050(G), 17.35.050(G), and 17.37.050(G) be amended to read, “No permanent structures near natural washes shall be built in the watercourse plus 75 feet from the center of the flowline, or a 50-foot buffer on either side, as measured out from the top of the wash, whichever is greater, to be determined by the City Engineer or designee. Additionally, no earthwork, excavation, or earth removal shall occur within the watercourse plus 75 feet from the center of the flowline, or a 50-foot buffer on either side of the top-of-bank as determined by determined by the City Engineer or designee.” Councilmember Clark seconded the motion Councilmember Wood moved to approve an Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Amending the Eagle Mountain Municipal Code Chapters 17.25 Residential Zones, 17.35 Commercial Zones, and 17.37 Business Park Zones with the following change: 1. The amendment in 17.25.050(G), 17.35.050(G), and 17.37.050(G) be amended to read, “No permanent structures near natural washes shall be built in the watercourse plus 75 feet from the center of the flowline, or a 50-foot buffer on either side, as measured out from the top of the wash, whichever is greater, to be determined by the City Engineer or designee. Additionally, no earthwork, excavation, or earth removal shall occur within the watercourse plus 75 feet from the center of the flowline, or a 50-foot buffer on either side of the top-of-bank as determined by determined by the City Engineer or designee.” Councilmember Clark seconded the motion. Topics: Parks & Recreation, Municipal Code Amendments.

docs.title: Triple Tail redevelopment plan adopted
docs.text: Triple Tail redevelopment plan adopted The city adopted the Triple Tail Community Reinvestment Project Area Plan, covering 24 parcels, to steer that land toward new development and economic uses. If you live near 4000 North and Pole Canyon Boulevard east of Tyson Parkway, or south of 1000 North east of Pony Express Parkway, expect the city to actively pursue development on the land around you. notable An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Adopting the Triple Tail Community Reinvestment Project Area Plan, as Approved by the Redevelopment Agency of Eagle Mountain City, as the Official Community Reinvestment Project Area Plan for the Project Area and Directing that Notice of the Adoption be Given as Required by Statute. Economic Development Director Evan Berrett presented the item. The proposed ordinance will allow for the creation of the Triple Tail Community Reinvestment Project Area. This Plan is the end result of a comprehensive evaluation of the types of appropriate land uses and economic development for the land, which lies within twenty-four parcels in the City. The north parcels are south of 4000 North, north of Pole Canyon Blvd, and east of Tyson Pkwy. The south parcel is south of 1000 North and east of Pony Express Pkwy. The Plan is intended to define the method and means of the Project Area from its current state to a higher and better use. Councilmember Wright moved to adopt an Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Adopting the Triple Tail Community Reinvestment Project Area Plan, as Approved by the Redevelopment Agency of Eagle Mountain City, as the Official Community Reinvestment Project Area Plan for the Project Area and Directing that Notice of the Adoption be Given as Required by Statute. docs.text: 672-acre development deal near the data centers The council took up a development agreement covering about 672 acres on two parcels, one near the Meta, Google, and QTS sites and one beside the Firefly area. This touches landowners and neighbors near the data center campuses and in the southwest near Firefly. The council rewrote the buffering language so it only binds land once that land is annexed into the city. notable An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Approving the Tract Development Agreement. City Attorney Marcus Draper presented the item. The proposed ordinance approves the Tract Development Agreement, which covers approximately 672 acres of land distributed among 2 different parcels. One of the parcels is located near the Meta, Google, and QTS sites. The other parcel abuts Industrial Planning Area 2 of the Firefly development in the southwestern portion of the City. Applicant representative Keely Ambrose addressed the Council regarding concerns around buffering, the addition of property, benchmarks, and length of the agreement. Councilmember Wood moved to adopt an Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Approving the Tract Development Agreement with the following change: 1. The last three sentences in Section 4.12 are removed and replaced with, “If Additional Property is annexed into this Agreement pursuant to this Section 4.12, then such future property shall be buffered as required by the Applicable Rules. This paragraph does not apply to any property located outside the City limits unless it is annexed into the City.” Councilmember Gray seconded the motion. Topics: Development Agreements.

Finance Management Analyst Terrence Dela Pena presented the item. Wayfinding signs currently exist throughout the City; these are deteriorating due to exposure to weather conditions and the usual wear and tear for their allowable functionality and appearance. The Citg's parking requirements have also been found to be excessive. Most cities require onlg one stall per sleeping unit, whereas Eagle Mountain requires one stall per bed which can greatlg increase the parking requirements if mang of the units have two queen beds or a similar format. While staff does not anticipate mang, if ang, motorhomes to park at hotels. The extra-long spaces are more likelg to be used bg vehicles with towed trailers, which is the target group staff was requested to trg and accommodate. However, trailer sizes can varg widelg, and depending on how theg are hooked up and what is loaded, maneuverabilitg can varg widelg as well. Using a Class A motorhome as a standard promotes long enough spaces and accommodation for vehicles that mag have a wide turn radius. The stalls are not required in the Commercial RegionalZone because it is more likelg that there would be adequate potential for shared parking from nearbg regional businesses with larger parking lots. Councilmember Clark noted the difficultg in comparing what is appropriate for the Citg with statistics from other cities due to the uniqueness of Eagle Mountain. She desires to balance attracting the best businesses with attracting which businesses are best for the Citg. Councilmember Burnham stated that residents might be more concerned about the appearance of the building than the height of the building. As the Citg has alreadg permitted four-storg buildings, she would prefer allowing additional height to accommodate higher-qualitg design aesthetics. Councilmember Wood recommended focusing on shorter product tgpes that fit more with the stgle of Eagle Mountain. He is against raising height standards. Councilmember Wright stated he recognizes the value of design standards and that theg should be considered in determining a height standard. Also, he feels that the parking stall requirements should take into account whether the hotel intends to offer extended stag accommodations. Mr. Berrett clarified that a partg had expressed interest in building a hotel in the Citg but had concerns about the hotel height and parking standards. Councilmember Grag advocated for establishing and enforcing a set height standard and being consistent and equitable for all use tgpes. Councilmember Wood concurred. Discussion ensued regarding the following: r The height and stgle of hotels the Citg desires; o Parking standard requirements and the benefits and issues that arise from permitting extended stag services; o The need for additional transportation services to support extended-stag hotels; o The benefits and potential issues with establishing a set height for all uses; and o Parking and turning radiuses for trailers, motorhomes, and buses. Magor Westmoreland opened the public hearing at 9:O2 p.m. As there were no comments, he closed the hearing. Mr. Berrett noted that the Citg is soliciting bids for and working on the Hotel Feasibilitg Studg and cost-sharing agreements to fund the studg. ln addition to familg members of residents, hotels are anticipated to be utilized bg business travelers supporting the ongoing development in the Citg. Hotels would allow the Citg to promote recreation and tourism. Councilmembers Clark and Wood suggested tabling the item and having it return after the Hotel Feasibilitg studg is completed. Councilmember Curtis and Mayor Pro Tempore Wright requested that discussion items be added to this section of the agenda regarding potential sections of Municipal Code being placed under review prior to Planning staff drafting the changes, in order to provide direction. Mr. Strachan noted that there are varying preferences regarding desired amendments and stated the importance of recognizing the particular roles assigned to each parfy. He advised the Council to staff to bring forth their best ideas, information, and practices, and make adjustments as the Council directs, but to not cut off the ideas before they come. Mayor Pro Tempore Wright stated that in light of the directives from the State, he has concerns with the nuances and flexibilities in Municipal Code, particularly with Title 16. As much as he respects the Planning Commission, they are not professional planners and it is at the purview of the Council to determine the review authority. He is nervous to grant broad discretion in some cases and advocated reviewing applicable instances in Titles 16 and 17. Administrator Items are intended to allow the Council to provide direction to staff as a body in a public setting. POLICY SESSION – CITY COUNCIL CHAMBERS ELECTED OFFICIALS PRESENT: Mayor Tom Westmoreland, Councilmembers Donna Burnham, Colby Curtis, Jared Gray, Carolyn Love, and Brett Wright. CITY STAFF PRESENT: Evan Berrett, Economic Development Director; Marcus Draper, City Attorney; Kimberly Ruesch, Finance Director; Tyler Maffitt, Communications Manager; Todd Black, Wildlife Biologist/Environmental Planner; Robert Hobbs, Planning Manager; David Stroud, Senior Planner; Steven Lehmitz, Planner; Fionnuala Kofoed, Director of Administrative Services/City Recorder; Chris Trusty, City Engineer; Brad Hickman, Parks and Recreation Director; Eric McDowell, Chief Deputy Sheriff; Bailey Ensign, Digital Communications Specialist; and Natalie Winterton, Grants Coordinator/Management Analyst. CALL TO ORDER Mayor Westmoreland called the policy session to order at 7:26 p.m. 5. PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE Resident Shelly Milne led the Pledge of Allegiance. 6. INFORMATION ITEMS/UPCOMING EVENTS • Eagle Mountain City will be offering spring dumpsters beginning Thursday, April 20 through Sunday, April 23. Residents are encouraged to dispose of items in the dumpsters. Residents with items that cannot be dumped will be provided with a pass to the Intermountain Regional Landfill in Fairfield. • Sandbag resources are being provided through Eagle Mountain City until flooding risks subside in the community. Interested residents can retrieve as many as 30 sandbags per household at City Hall or the Community Development building. Sand is available at White Hills Park, the Rodeo Grounds, North Ranch Park and Silverlake Park. • Homeowners are encouraged to wait before watering their lawns for the year. Help the City achieve its water conservation goals while better managing our water utility systems. Wait to water until temperatures are consistently warmer. • Residents who don’t use social media to stay in touch with the City are encouraged to sign up for the City’s text notification system. Weekly, the City sends updates on news, important information, and sign-ups for recreational sports. Learn more at eaglemountaincity.com. 7. PUBLIC COMMENTS Mayor Westmoreland opened public comment at 7:30 p.m. Jim Smith expressed appreciation to Zac Hilton and the Streets Department for their quick response to weather impacts on roads. Bruno Hunziker inquired regarding the status of the money the City lost due to fraud and requested mitigation of traffic delays caused by additional traffic lights. The City Administrator stated that City representatives will be meeting with the insurance company regarding negotiations of an unsatisfactory offer associated with the recent fraud loss. The FBI investigation is ongoing. An outside forensic team determined the breech was not in the City’s system. Regarding transportation, staff will be meeting with Mountainland Association of Governments and the City lobbyist is working to get funds allocated to transportation needs. Mayor Westmoreland closed public comment at 7:40 p.m. 8. CITY COUNCIL/MAYOR’S ITEMS Councilmember Love Councilmember Love welcomed the public and thanked them for their insights. She recognized City employees for flood prevention and the first responders for emergency response to the accident in Pole Canyon. Councilmember Wright Councilmember Wright thanked the residents for attending and being involved in the process of government. The Pact Act passed by Congress provides additional benefits to veterans who were exposed to certain toxins during their service. American Legion #111 Post Commander Jeff Ruth is available to assist veterans with filling out the associated paperwork. The Legion plan to install a banner with the suicide prevention phone number at a local baseball field. Councilmember Gray Councilmember Gray echoed appreciation to the meeting participants and Streets Department. He thanked the Volunteers in Police Service for their service in controlling the runoff and keeping the citizens safe. He recognized Utah House of Representative Stephanie Gricius and Eagle Mountain Chamber of Commerce President Melissa Clark in attendance at the meeting. Councilmember Burnham Councilmember Burnham thanked Representative Gricius for working with the City Administrator to protect Eagle Mountain from being targeted by a State Department with restrictions only subject to Eagle Mountain City. The City needs Youth Council Advisors. She appreciates the residents attending the meeting and said that the Council hears and listens to their concerns and cares. Councilmember Curtis Councilmember Curtis thanked those in attendance. Mayor Westmoreland Mayor Westmoreland recognized Utah House of Representative Stephanie Gricius, Eagle Mountain Chamber of Commerce President Melissa Clark, and the citizens present and expressed appreciation for their meeting participation. 9. APPOINTMENT 9.A. Director of Legislative Affairs 1. Clifford Strachan

The tower shall be allowed to be a 100-foot tall monolithic cell tower instead of a light pole in the location desired and be configured as shown on the submitted plans; 2. An emergency backup generator shall be approved to be a part of the tower’s equipment. Councilmember Gray seconded the motion. docs.title: An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Amending the Eagle Mountain Municipal Code, Chapters 10.10 Parking. Grants Coordinator/Management Analyst Natalie Winterton reviewed the changes requested by the City Council during the work session that differ from the proposed amendment in the packet materials: 1. 10.10.30 – It is unlawful to leave any vehicle parked continuously on a public street for longer than 72 hours without being moved having been driven a distance of at least 400 feet before returning to the same location; 2. 10.10.090(B) – “Commercial vehicle” means a tractor or motor vehicle at or exceeding a rated capacity of 2.5 tons, trailer, or semi-trailer used or maintained for the transportation of persons or property that operates: 1. As a carrier for hire, compensation, or profit; 2. As a carrier to transport the vehicle owner’s goods or property in furtherance of the owner’s commercial enterprise; or 3. As a food cart or food truck; 3. 10.10.090(F)(5) – remove completely and adjust the numbering accordingly rather than removing van and adding boat as presented in the packet materials; and 4. 10.10.100(A)(2) – Agricultural vehicle, recreational vehicle, or occupied or empty trailer, within the front yard area (excluding a paved or gravel driveway) of any residential zone of the city. Ms. Winterton clarified that she had discussed the definitions of commercial vehicles with the Planning Commission in regard to a different amendment. Changes to this chapter do not require Planning Commission review. Councilmember Gray suggested allowing commercial vehicles up to 2.5 tons and amending the prohibition to state vehicles over 2.5 tons. The Council supported amending EMMC 10.10.090(B) to a “vehicle exceeding a rated capacity of 2.5 tons.” Councilmember Wright confirmed with Mayor Westmoreland that he is comfortable with the enforcement of the proposed changes.

docs.title: An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Adopting the Eagle Mountain City Transportation Master Plan. City Engineer Chris Trusty presented the changes as discussed during the work session. Councilmember Wright recommended tabling the item to resolve concerns and finalize details. Councilmember Love said she sees no need for Old Airport Road to follow the proposed trajectory if the future freeway is being relocated. She would like to review and better understand the impacts of the proposed changes in alignment before approving the plan and agrees that it would be beneficial to have Old Airport Road and the future freeway lined with commercial uses, open space, or decorative features to provide buffering for residential areas. Discussion ensued regarding uncertainty with land acquisition, the potential need to abandon certain areas of the road once the freeway is completed, and possible solutions. Mr. Trusty stated that he is unable to move forward with the impact fees facility plan until the Transportation Master Plan is approved and a landowner has been waiting on the finalization of the plan to be able to sell property. He recognized the Council’s desire to get the details of the plan correct but noted master plans generally exclude the finer details of the projects. He confirmed that the Council will be reviewing and voting upon the expansion of Old Airport Road independent of this approval. It might prove beneficial to contact the property owners to evaluate the likelihood of the City being able to purchase the land necessary to change the alignment. Mayor Westmoreland explained the challenges the City faces with future transportation in this area for Old Airport Road and the future freeway. Discussion determined to table the item and to assign two Councilmembers to work with staff and the consultants on amending the plan.

docs.title: A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Adopting the Eagle Mountain City Vision Statement, Mission Statement, and Strategic Goals. Economic Development Director Evan Berrett presented the item and reviewed the elements of strategic planning. Staff and the City Council determined to review the mission statement at a future meeting and discussed and amended the draft vision and strategic goals as follows: Vision: Eagle Mountain is a safe, growing city with a small town feel that serves families and individuals by creating reliable services and infrastructure, cultivating economic and recreational opportunities, and harmonizing protected space with the flourishing of all life. Strategic Goals: 1. Diverse Economic Growth. Eagle Mountain is home to businesses of all sizes spanning several industries resulting in an expanded tax base, convenient access for all residents to essential goods and services, and growth of employment opportunities for workers at any stage of their careers. 2. Robust Infrastructure Networks. Eagle Mountain has expanded its infrastructure capacities to comfortably accommodate the demands of a larger population by improving transportation connections and infrastructure standards alongside state and regional partners, augmenting network capabilities, and implementing maintenance and replacement programs for all infrastructure. 3. Unique Reputational Evolution. Eagle Mountain is known and respected for its commitments toward, and achievements in, meeting the expectations of residents through efforts to embrace its family-centric and rural heritage, engaging in creative solutions to address resident needs, and its contributions to the prosperity of the state. 4. Proactive Generational Planning. Eagle Mountain is a balanced, intergenerational city that has proactively managed its growth, resulting in quality home-ownership opportunities for residents; a redundant and reliable water supply; and gathering places and amenities that provide for the social, educational, recreational, and health care needs of its residents. 5. Interactive Environmental Stewardship. Eagle Mountain has interlaced the preservation of the natural environment; the protection of native wildlife; and the promotion of outdoor recreation through the expansion of permanent, convenient, and interconnected trail networks; conservation of open spaces and natural features; and protection of historic sites significant to our heritage 6. Dynamic Service Enhancement. Eagle Mountain is a full-service community that delivers extraordinary services and amenities to residents by attracting and retaining passionate employees, innovating throughout the organization to increase efficiency and remain fiscally conservative, and developing highly responsive communication channels to improve resident experiences.

docs.title: A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Approving the Amended and Restated Porter's Crossing Town Center Master Development Agreement (MDA). This item was removed from the agenda at the applicant’s request. 16. MOTION 16.A. MOTION – Consideration of Waiver of Tax Clearance for the Dedication of Public Open Space. Councilmember Curtis stated his understanding was that the City could only accept the dedication of land free from any encumbrance. He is uncomfortable making a goodwill gesture with tax money paid by the residents. Councilmember Gray acknowledged that although he does not feel the City is to blame, neither does he think the applicant is completely at fault, as they were required to clean up debris left by other people. Councilmember Burnham conceded Councilmember Gray’s point but agreed with concerns about passing the expense of the developer’s taxes to residents. Councilmember Wright said while he appreciates the applicant resolving the issue, the agreement with the City required the dedication of the land. Nevertheless, the applicant had the ability to monitor and mitigate the taxes compared to the residents that had no ability to weigh in on the issue. Councilmember Love said she understands the desire to offer a gesture of goodwill to the developer; however, it would set a precedence that could become problematic. Councilmember Gray clarified that his intention is not to pay the taxes but to show courtesy and properly credit the developer for their positive contributions to the City during interactions on future projects.

docs.title: An Ordinance of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Enacting Eagle Mountain Municipal Code Chapter 2.17 Appointed Officers, and Amending Eagle Mountain Municipal Code Chapter 2.27 Board Appointment Process. Ms. Kofoed reviewed the item as presented during work session. She read the email Councilmember Curtis sent to the Council that was mentioned during work session with his suggested changes to the amendment. The Council discussed the proposed amendment and determined to approve the following changes: • EMMC 2.17.010 Process for Appointing Officers – In accordance with Utah Code Ann. § 10-3-9, the mayor, with the advice and consent of the city council, shall appoint a qualified person to the office of city recorder, city treasurer, city attorney and city engineer. If Eagle Mountain City creates a municipal fire or police department, the police chief and fire chief shall also be appointed officers. All appointed officers shall continue in office until their successors are appointed and qualified. All appointments of officers designated herein shall follow the process as outlined in EMMC 2.27 Appointment Process. • EMMC Chapter 2.27 Appointment Process: o 2.27.010 Definitions - “Statutorily appointed” shall mean any position designated in EMMC 2.17.010 Appointed Officers. o 2.27.020 Appointment – Unless otherwise designated, the mayor shall appoint all advisory board members, statutorily appointed officers, and planning commission members with the advice and consent of the city council. o 2.27.030 Posting of Positions – Notice of all empty or expiring advisory board, statutorily appointed positions, or planning commission members shall be posted on the city webpage, or other method suitable to provide notice to the public, for a minimum of ten days. The notice shall include a description of the position and provide details for the submission of an application or resume for the position. The mayor shall compile and evaluate all applications or resumes for the position. o 2.27.040 Notice to Council – Not less than three (3) days prior to publicly noticing the possible appointment or reappointment of any person to an advisory board, planning commission, or statutorily appointed position, the mayor shall provide to each member of the city council the name, and application or resume if available, of each person the mayor is considering appointing to an advisory board, planning commission, or statutorily appointed position. Members of the city council may individually provide the mayor with feedback or recommendations regarding each potential appointment. o 2.27.050 Removal – An advisory board or planning commission member may be removed with or without cause by the mayor with the advice and consent of the city council.

docs.title: A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Adopting the Public Infrastructure District Policy. Councilmember Curtis expressed concern with the risks associated with Public Infrastructure Districts (PIDs), allowing developers to oversee resident taxes, and the potential abuse of inflated reimbursement rates. As he has no intention of applying a PID to a residential development, he would prefer not to have associated standards in Municipal Code. Councilmembers Wright and Love concurred with not approving PIDs for residential developments. Mayor Westmoreland noted the benefit of the additional oversight and risk reduction measures of invested parties. City Attorney Jeremy Cook clarified the reason for placing the item on the agenda was to identify Council concerns to be able to address the issues and establish approval criteria in the governing document. Section 4 provides for the Council to deny a PID for any reason. PIDs could allow for improvements desired in the City that would otherwise be not viable financially. Discussion ensued regarding concerns regarding: • The impact of the cost of the PID on house affordability; • The potential for homebuyers to not understand the higher tax rate when purchasing their home; • The impact on the ability of residents to sell their homes; • The PID cost increasing as the value of the home increases; • Development funding mechanisms; • Placing the burden of improvements and benefits to the overall City on a specific group of residents; and • Details of the bond payments. Councilmember Love requested additional information regarding commercial PIDs. City Administrator Paul Jerome recommended any PIDs approved in the City have an economic development component. He does not foresee a circumstance in which the City would find a residential PID to be beneficial.
