docs.text: Table the Cedar Førms rezone and preliminary plat until the meeting directly following the City… Commissioner Gray moved to table the Cedar Førms rezone and preliminary plat until the meeting directly following the City Council's øpproval of the new residentíøI ordinønce. Commíssioner Wright seconded the motion. Those votíng øye: Møtthew Everett, DeLín Anderson, Brett Wright, Rich Wood, and Jared Grøy. The motíon pøssed wíth s unanimous vote. 5.8 Chapter 17.80 (Sigr Regulations and Sign Permits) - Development Code Amendment, Public Hearing Mr. Jensen said the applicant-proposed Development Code amendment will allow flagpoles up to 50 feet tall at model homes. The current Code allows flagpoles up to 20 feet tall. Applicant Jessica Eddington with Edge Homes said homes stand up to 25 feet tall in the City and they would like to be able to fly the American flag above the homes. Commissioner Everett asked why she is proposing this for model homes only, and not for the entire City. Commissioner Gray stated the maximum square footage of the flag will remain at forty square feet for the American flag and fifteen square feet for all others. Ms. Eddington said they are proposing the amendment in this portion of Municipal Code because it applies directly to Edge Homes as they would like to put American flags at their model homes. Commissioner Wood said he is concerned that the proposed amendment does not limit flags on fifty-foot flagtrloles specifically to the American flag. He expressed concerns that Edge homes may fly their flags on fifty-foot poles. Commissioner Wright said model homes can install up to six flagpoles and expressed concern that the amendment would allow six fifty-foot flagtrloles. Mr. Hadley clarified that the limitation is six flags. Ms. Eddington said the American flag should be flown above all other flags, and the intention is not to fly Edge Homes flags as high as the American flag. Eagle Mountain Planning Commission Meeting - April23,2019 PageTofll Commissioner Wood said he understands that, but as this is a City-wide amendment, other companies may not fly the American flag as Edge Homes will. Commissioner Everett opened the public hearing at 6:30 p.m. As there were no comments, he closed the hearing. Commissioner Wood said he would like to allow model homes to fly the American flag. He asked what happens to the flagpoles once model homes are sold. Commissioner Gray explained the building code states that buildings cannot exceed 35 feet. He said 50 feet is too high for a flagpole. Since the American flag should fly higher than other flags, he would approve a height limit of 35 feet for American flags and 30 feet for other flags. Mr. Jensen said flagtrloles are defined as ancillary structures in Municipal Code. The height limits are different through the different densities and are typically 20 feet. Discussion ensued regarding flag poles located at previous model homes in the City. Commissioner Everett said he appreciates the desire to give prominence to the American Flag, but feels 50 feet is too tall. He expressed concern that this is specific to model homes and said it is appropriate to address this change in other sections of Municipal Code, as residents also desire to fly the Americanflag. He said a resident may choose to fly a flag that is offensive to other residents, although he would defend that resident's right to fly a flag of their choosing under their First Amendment rights. He asked if it is better to change the amendment to only apply to the American flag. Commissioner 'W'ood said it may be more appropriate to allow a larger flagtrlole at entrances to developments, but stated 50 feet is too tall. He said the model home portion of Municipal Code is the wrong section to amend. Mr. Jensen said taller flags could be provided in parks, as other amenities can be proposed by developers. He said staffs opinion is that 50 feet is too tall in residential neighborhoods, especially as they don't know what will be flown after the model home is sold. Another staff concern is that using the Americanflag for advertising is against the United States Flag Code. Discussion ensued regarding the height of existing flag¡loles in surrounding cities, and the number of allowed flags in areas with multiple model homes. Commissioner Gray said the American flag should be flown higher than other flags, and 35 feet is appropriate, with other flags at 30 feet. He said increasing the flagpole height is a legitimate change, and stated he would like the Municipal Code to require all but one flagtrlole need to be removed once a model home is sold. Eagle Mountain Planning Commission Meeting - April 23,2019 PageSofll Commissioner Wood said this is the wrong section in the Municipal Code for this amendment. He said there are more appropriate places to display the American flag, and the Code needs to designate a location on residential properties for flags. Mr. Jensen said staff can bring additional changes to flag and flagpole restrictions to a future meeting. Commissioner Wood said he is not in favor of approving the amendment and stated the City does not want to allow builders to fly flags over model homes. He said residential areas are not appropriate places for flags. Commissioner Gray recommended approving the amendment with changes stating the American flag can be flown on 35-foot flagpoles, other flags on 3O-foot poles, and all but one flagpole must be removed at the sale of the model home. He said staff can create an amendment that applies to the remaining areas of the City. Commissioner Wright stated he is not in favor of moving forward with the proposed amendment at this time, but is open to a well-researched staff-proposed amendment. Mr. Hadley said the Planning Commission can table the item and direct the applicant to work with staff to adjust the proposed amendment according to the Commission's feedback. If the Commission recommends denial, the item will go to City Council for further consideration. Discussion ensued regarding potential amendments to the Municipal Code regarding flags, and what the current Code requires regarding ancillary structures. Mr. Hadley recommended the Commissioners make a decision on the current item and allow the flag discussion to come back at a future meeting. Commissioner V/right asked if they can table the item but allow one flagtrlole to be taller than currently allowed. Mr. Hadley explained the best way forward is to make a recommendation to the City Council based specifically on information the applicant has provided. Topics: Zoning & Land Use, Development Agreements, Municipal Code Amendments.

The motíon pøssed with a unønímous vote. 5 Action and Advisory Items 5.A. Cedar Farms - Rezone and Preliminary Plat, Public Hearing Mr. Jensen explained the applicant is proposing to rezone 5.47 acres from Agriculture to Residential. The preliminary plat is a two-lot subdivision with a minimum lot size of 2.5 acres. Items to consider include the General Plan designation, compatibility, impact on City services, traffic generation, property value impact, and lot frontage and zoning standards. Mr. Jensen explained the proposal complies with the General Plan, is compatible with surrounding land uses, complies with lot frontage and zoning standards, and is not anticipated to burden City services, have an impact on traffic or on property values. Commissioner Gray asked if the powerline corridors are dedicated to the City as open space and if the future road is a concern regarding the utility corridors. Mr. Jensen said utility easements can be either dedicated to the City, or included in lots, and staff is not concerned with the future road as it is not included in this plan. Applicant Karen Scott said most people cannot afford five acres of land, so they have decided to split the property into two lots to make them more affordable. Commissioner Everett opened the public hearing at 6:13 p.m. As there were no comments, he closed the hearíng. Commissioner Everett asked where the powerlines are located. Mr. Jensen said they are in the rear of the property. Any building that takes place on the lots will be outside of the easements, but the lots still contain large building pads. Commissioner Wood said he and Commissioner Gray visited the site, and it is important to note thaf a future road is planned on this property. Commissioner Gray also expressed concerns about the road. Mr. Jensen clarified that the future road will actually be west of the propose d rezone area. Applicant Jeff Scott conf,rrmed the future road will be approximately 100 feet behind the property, outside of the utility corridor. Commissioner Anderson asked staff if they have concerns regarding the gas easements. Mr. Jensen said they do not as any future structures will need to comply with the gas company's requirements for building over easements. Commissioner Wood stated City Attomey Jeremy Cook recommended against rezoning until the new residential zones are in place. He said since the City does not have a zoningmap yet, there is no way to determine what requirements and setbacks will apply. Eagle Mountain Planning Commission Meeting - April23,2019 Page6of11 Mr. Jensen explained the proposed rezone does comply with the General Plan. The proposed setbacks follow the base density setbacks, which are not changing in the amended residential zones. Commissioner Wright said details such as property setbacks and building envelopes are not defined as of yet. Commissioner Gray said it may be June at the latest when the amended zones are approved. He recommended that the item be tabled until the new zones are in place. Topics: Zoning & Land Use, Development Agreements, Public Works & Infrastructure, Parks & Recreation.

docs.title: Community Services Board Meeting — 2026-07-22 (minutes not yet published)
docs.text: Meeting of 2026-07-22. The minutes for this meeting have not been published yet, so the site has no motion list or roll-call record for it — the account below comes from the meeting recording and its transcript. **In short:** The Community Services Board spent most of this meeting building Eagle Mountain's application for a state "Healthy Utah Community" designation, settling on nine things the city already does and three new commitments for the next three years. Members also shaped two birthday-year events, a month-long fitness challenge and a 30-backpack treasure hunt, and began designing the rules for handing out RAP tax grant money. Only two votes were taken: approving past minutes and adjourning. **Present:** Jessie Southworth (chair), Melissa Clark (City Council), Zac Huish (City Council), Mare Burningham, Cherie Curtis, Jay Johnson, and Charlotte Ducos, who arrived roughly 45 minutes in and asked to be noted in the minutes. Steve Conger and Liz were excused. **Staff:** Steve Mumford (staff liaison, presented the Healthy Utah and America 250 items), Jason Hall (Recreation), Don Hamm (Events), Soraya Farmer (digital communications specialist, attending in place of Kyle Ireland). ## Decisions | # | Agenda ref | Motion | Moved / Seconded | Vote | Result | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | 2 | Approve the minutes of the previous two meetings — the June regular meeting and the special meeting on recreation sponsorships — with one correction, that the minutes render Mare Burningham's first name as "Mayor" | Moved by Cherie Curtis / seconded by Mare Burningham | Voice vote | Passed | | 2 | 9 | Adjourn, at 8:28 PM | Moved by Charlotte Ducos / seconded by Zac Huish | Voice vote | Passed | **Settled without a vote:** - Recreation soccer jerseys will be printed without a number on the front, saving about $1,000 of a roughly $12,000 order; the board treated the final call as Jason Hall's design decision and agreed the number can be added back next year if parents complain. - Requests for help from the communications team will travel from board members to the chair, then to Steve Mumford, then to communications — the board advises rather than directs city communications, and individual members will not send requests directly. - Communications will design a Community Services Board banner and logo so the board can identify itself at booths, ideally in time for the August 1 back-to-school event. - Banner sponsorships will be promoted on LinkedIn rather than Facebook, framed as helping children play rather than as a request for money, with the recreation department's shared email as the contact rather than a staff member's personal address. - Unauthorized banners in parks and routine maintenance problems should be reported through the city app rather than raised at board meetings. - Steve Mumford will get cost estimates from the Parks Department for the board's eight-item priority list and bring it to a City Council work session with a dollar figure and an eligible funding source beside each item. - The board identified nine strategies Eagle Mountain already has in place for the Healthy Utah application and committed to three new ones over three years: joining the Communities That Care coalition, starting an adaptive sports program with Special Olympics as the longer-term aspiration, and adding trail wayfinding signs showing time and distance alongside a campaign telling residents where the trails are. - The board declined to pursue a tax on sugar-sweetened beverages, one of the options on the state's list. - Steve Mumford will draft the Healthy Utah letter of commitment, send it to the chair to review, then forward it to the City Council, which would formally designate the board as the city's health coalition by resolution. The application is due in August. - An informal group — Steve Mumford, Mare Burningham, Melissa Clark, Jessie Southworth, with Jay Johnson researching — will study what a community garden actually requires and bring recommendations to the City Council. - The August event will be a "Walk 30" or "Move 30" challenge, deliberately loose: 30 miles, or 30 of nearly anything active. Everyone who finishes goes into a drawing, and Melissa Clark will ask Anytime Fitness whether it will donate a one-year membership as the prize. - September's treasure hunt will run on Wednesday evenings and Saturdays, with Steve Mumford working out the staffing and the exact time of day. City staff, their families, and elected officials will be ineligible. - RAP tax grant criteria will be built over several meetings rather than one, starting at the next meeting with the Parks and Recreation scoring rubric. The board wants the program in place by January. - The board will staff a booth at the August 1 back-to-school night, using safe routes to school as its angle for gathering resident input. - The amendment allowing remote participation in meetings was pushed to a future agenda. ## Meeting map | Agenda ref | Topic | ~Start (elapsed) | One-line note | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Call to order and roll call | 0:00 | Called to order at 6:03 PM; members stated their names in turn. | | 2 | Approval of minutes | 0:32 | Two sets of minutes approved with one name correction. | | 3–4 | Recap and project updates | 2:09 | Jersey numbers, sponsorship outreach, off-street trails, and the board's priority list. | | 5 | Communications team | 23:46 | Soraya Farmer introduced herself and set out how the team can help. | | 6 | Healthy Utah Community Designation | 41:34 | The longest item; picked nine existing and three new health strategies. | | 7 | America 250 / Eagle Mountain 30 | 1:24:26 | Walk 30, the 30-backpack treasure hunt, and the fall events calendar. | | 8a | RAP tax funding criteria | 1:52:22 | Early design of the grant application, rubric, and review process. | | 8b | Board comments and announcements | 2:16:41 | Booth plans, the volunteer policy update, and remote participation. | | 9 | Adjournment | 2:25:02 | Adjourned at 8:28 PM. | **Discussed but NOT on the agenda:** community gardens as a land-use and open-space question, an unauthorized football banner on the pickleball courts, the city's scorpion hunts, and whether RAP tax money can be banked across years. **On agenda but little/no discussion:** the 9/11 Day of Service and the rules-of-order amendment for remote participation, both carried to a future meeting. ## What was discussed ### 2 — Approval of minutes Two sets of minutes were before the board: the June regular meeting and a special meeting held to approve recreation sponsorships. The only correction raised was that the minutes had written Mare Burningham's first name as "Mayor," a mistake she said happens constantly — "It's one syllable." The motion passed on a voice vote. ### 3–4 — Recap and ongoing projects The largest thread was the recreation soccer jerseys. Steve Mumford explained that the vendor's quote came to nearly $12,000 with a number printed on the front of each jersey, and that dropping that number would save about $1,000, because the front is a separate press. Mare Burningham said she preferred the front number as a spectator, since it makes players identifiable whichever way they run. Cherie Curtis agreed the number matters more for older players on crowded fields, but not for five-a-side games with small children. Charlotte Ducos reframed the question: how many more children could be sponsored with that $1,000? That argument carried the room. The board's consensus was to print without the number, treat it as Jason Hall's decision to finalize, and add it back next year if parents object. Sponsorship work is not finished. All the jersey sponsorships are covered, but banner sponsorships are not, and the chair asked members to keep approaching businesses. The board decided to advertise on LinkedIn rather than Facebook, on Melissa Clark's point that businesses look for these opportunities there, and agreed with Charlotte Ducos that the pitch should be "help kids play" rather than "sponsor us," so the city does not read as needy. Steve Mumford reported that the off-street trails master plan had been approved the previous night. He has been working with Ty Shepherd of the Lake Mountain Trails Association, and a memorandum of understanding with SITLA that would give the city legal access to trails in the Hidden Valley area went over to the agency the night before. The association would take on most trail maintenance, and this year plans to focus on the safety and rideability of existing trails rather than cutting new ones. Zac Huish's assessment of the timeline: "Just imagine like the slowest government possible and then multiply it by 10." The board also pressed on what happened to the priority list it produced last month. Steve Mumford said it had only gone out as an email update to the council and mayor. Zac Huish asked what would make it actionable and answered his own question — estimated costs beside each project. Melissa Clark first suggested holding the list until after August 18 because of existing criticism about city spending, then reversed herself once she understood the list was small, quick items such as benches and two parks that are not compliant with the Americans with Disabilities Act. Those, she noted, could be covered with leftover Community Development Block Grant funds: "let's ADA this place on up." Steve Mumford will bring costs and funding sources to a council work session. ### 5 — Communications team Soraya Farmer, the city's digital communications specialist, came in place of Kyle Ireland to introduce herself and ask how her team could help. She offered photography, video, blog posts, calendar listings, and newsletter space, asking only for as much lead time as possible — ideally two weeks. The substantive outcome was a workflow. Steve Mumford was direct that what the city does not want is individual board members telling the communications department what to post, since the board is advisory. Melissa Clark argued requests should route through the chair so that the chair can always answer for what the board is doing publicly. The agreed path runs from members to Jessie Southworth to Steve Mumford to communications, with Steve Mumford adding that people can copy him and the chair at the same time to avoid a game of telephone. Two asks came out of the discussion: a banner and logo so the board can identify itself at public events, and a design template so sponsor banners on the pickleball courts look consistent. Melissa Clark also proposed featuring board members in the city's social media reels to give the RAP tax a human face during the gap before any funded project exists, and Charlotte Ducos suggested that completed RAP tax projects carry a plate reading that residents' RAP tax dollars paid for them. ### 6 — Healthy Utah Community Designation This was the meeting's main work. The state designation requires a city to identify nine strategies it already has in place, three in each of three categories, and commit to at least three new ones over the following three years. Melissa Clark, who said she had been asking for this designation for three years, noted the city already does most of what the list asks. Working from a handout, the board assembled the existing nine: for active living, the Turkey Trot, Safe Routes to School, the newly approved off-street trails master plan, the bike and pedestrian master plan, and the city's Wellness Wednesdays; for healthy eating, a farmers market that accepts SNAP benefits, the library's seed exchange and food pantry, and ordinances permitting backyard poultry; for mental health, naloxone access, free gun locks at the library, the medication drop box, Believer City status, the Motivational Mile, and senior lunches and bingo. A recurring question was whether a plan counts once approved or only once built — the board leaned on approval being enough, since it had more than three candidates in every category regardless. One option was rejected outright. Reading down the list, Melissa Clark hit the sugar-sweetened beverage tax and said, "I'm a hard no on this one... I don't drink sugar, but still, no, hard pass." The three new commitments took longer. Jessie Southworth proposed joining the Communities That Care coalition, a prevention program the city participated in years ago through a coordinator shared with Saratoga Springs, and which lapsed when the staffer left. She argued there is a large gap in the city's mental health resources. Steve Mumford will contact Saratoga Springs to learn what the city had to do to take part. The second came from a resident who approached the board at the farmers market about adaptive sports; Melissa Clark's daughters had been on a Special Olympics bocce team that won a state silver medal, and the board settled on an adaptive sports program with Special Olympics as the aspiration. The third combines trail wayfinding signs showing time and distance with a campaign telling residents where the trails are — Charlotte Ducos noted that people hike Turtle Hill but many residents do not know what Turtle Hill is, and Mare Burningham asked for trails to be graded by ability so families with strollers or wheelchairs can find suitable routes. Community gardens came up as a possible commitment and were set aside precisely because the board did not want to promise something it had not researched. The discussion was substantial anyway. Melissa Clark said the city had tried edible gardens before to check a box and they were "just garbage within a year," and that the answer is requirements: if the board works out what a community garden actually needs, the council could adopt it as an alternative to the pool that multifamily developments are currently required to build, or grant open-space credit for it. Charlotte Ducos argued the gardens belong where residents lack their own land — apartments and condominiums. Zac Huish raised maintenance, warning against scattering small plots a parks technician would have to remember. Don Hamm noted the senior center already has garden boxes that residents use, and more could be added along that stretch of trail. ### 7 — America 250 / Eagle Mountain 30 Steve Mumford proposed a "Walk 30" for August, modeled on the national Walk 250. Charlotte Ducos suggested "Move 30," and the concept loosened from there into 30 of nearly anything active — walking 30 dogs, a group of 30 walking together. Participants would submit a photo or video through a simple form, with entries going into a drawing rather than being judged, after Cherie Curtis pointed out that judging the "most original" entry raised the question of who judges. Melissa Clark suggested asking Anytime Fitness to donate a one-year membership, which would give the sponsor real publicity, and volunteered to take part in her eagle costume. The treasure hunt is larger. Thirty backpacks will be hidden across the city, and Steve Mumford passed one around: a water bottle, a 30th anniversary hat, an America 250 fanny pack, a t-shirt, sunglasses, a lapel pin, a keychain, stickers, and a city-branded pickleball paddle. Suggestions came quickly — a book from the library with a card promotion, mini binoculars and a wildlife guide, black-light pen lights for scorpion hunting, and contributions from the Chamber, the Wildlife Alliance, and the Arts Alliance so the bags read as community partnership rather than city merchandise. The scheduling question was left partly open. Steve Mumford laid out options from one backpack a day for 30 days to all 30 at once. The board converged on Wednesday evenings and Saturdays, then complicated it: soccer games run Saturday mornings from August 15, so afternoons may be better. Steve Mumford took the logistics away to solve. Everyone who arrives within the window gets a shirt and sticker even though only one person gets the backpack, and city staff, their families, and elected officials will be ineligible. Don Hamm gave the sharpest warning of the night about site selection: do not forget a drop in White Hills, a neighborhood he described as feeling excluded from the city — "You will be hung." Don Hamm also walked through the fall calendar: the summer bash and fireworks that Saturday, which drew 20,000 people last year; a back-to-school clothing swap on August 1; Shop Fest, Prep Fest and the 9/11 Day of Service in September; Halloween Town, an adaptive trick-or-treat, a movie in the park and the half marathon on October 3; and the Turkey Trot and Veterans Breakfast in November. He offered to send the board a calendar marking where volunteers are needed. ### 8a — RAP tax funding criteria The board began designing how it will award RAP tax grant money, with a target of having the process settled by January. Melissa Clark described Lehi's model, where 70 percent of funds go to council- and city-designated projects and 30 percent to grants. Charlotte Ducos objected to fixing any percentage, arguing the board should judge projects on merit rather than against a quota — a genuinely strong community project should not be turned away because a bucket is full. Melissa Clark's counter was that unlimited flexibility could let a single project consume most of a year's funds, and she proposed tiers instead, with a higher bar for larger requests. Zac Huish supported keeping room for something ambitious, raising the group that wants to build a recreation center as the kind of project that might be worth one big allocation in a year. Several design points drew agreement. Applications should require the number of people served, the number of volunteers involved, cost information, and a specific plan for acknowledging RAP tax funding. Projects must have a presence in Eagle Mountain rather than merely operating in the region — Melissa Clark described a theater group in another city seeking Lehi money because two Lehi residents attended, and called it a "hard no." Melissa Clark, drawing on writing and reviewing grants, argued the application should be standardized enough that inexperienced organizations are not outplayed by those who know how to work the process. City projects and community projects will be assessed separately, or through one application with conditional sections, since the board cannot realistically score a city trail project against a neighborhood request. The board liked rubric language that ends in "defer or revise" rather than denial, and agreed any denial needs a written explanation and an invitation to reapply. Melissa Clark noted RAP tax funds can be banked toward a future project, though not turned into a permanent endowment. The next meeting starts with the Parks and Recreation rubric. ### 8b — Board comments and announcements The board decided to staff a booth at the August 1 back-to-school event, where Don Hamm said 2,600 people attended last year, using safe routes to school as the theme and collecting reports through the city app. Don Hamm gave a concrete example: children in one neighborhood walk along Eagle Mountain Boulevard where no trail exists and the city cannot connect one because it does not own the land. Charlotte Ducos asked whether running the board's booth next to her student council booth at Shop Fest would be a conflict; Melissa Clark said no, since no money changes hands. Steve Mumford reported that a volunteer program meeting had taken place with Melissa Clark, Charlotte Ducos, Jessie Southworth, Don Hamm, and communications, and that management interns Ethan and Addie are drafting policy to bring back to the board. The amendment allowing remote participation was deferred, though Steve Mumford noted the room's new system now supports it. ## Notable moments - **A late arrival, on the record.** Roughly 45 minutes in, Charlotte Ducos interrupted to ask whether she needed to note that she had entered. "Charlotte Ducos is here." The chair had also meant to excuse Steve Conger and Liz at the start and had forgotten. - **The minutes misspelled a name into a title.** The single correction to two meetings' minutes was that "Mare" had been written as "Mayor" — which is also why the recording is full of references to "Mayor" that mean a board member, not the city's mayor. - **$1,000 reframed as children.** Charlotte Ducos turned a design debate about jersey numbers into a budget question in one sentence — how many more kids could play for that money — and the room shifted immediately. - **Technology did not cooperate.** Steve Mumford's laptop would not drive the display and the printer was uncooperative, so the meeting's central item was run largely from memory and a paper handout. Melissa Clark: "We know you can't print." - **A movie credit surfaced.** A digression established that Jay Johnson appeared in a film, which drew the observation that this is why he is on the board — "for the star power." - **Do not skip White Hills.** Don Hamm's warning about leaving that neighborhood out of the treasure hunt was the most emphatic advice of the evening, grounded in a previous giveaway. - **Scorpions are a civic asset.** The city's scorpion hunt has run four times and packed the building, prompting a suggestion to advertise a habitat-restoration planting day as a scorpion hunt to boost turnout. ## About this transcript This is an automated transcription with automated speaker separation, and names were assigned afterward from evidence inside the recording — people stating their own names, members addressing each other, and the chair naming who moved and seconded. The published agenda independently corroborates that Steve Mumford led the Healthy Utah and America 250 items. Speaker separation found nine distinct voices for the eleven people present. Jay Johnson and Jason Hall speak rarely, and some of their remarks are attributed to Zac Huish and Don Hamm respectively. Long stretches of speech are reliably attributed; one- and two-word interjections are the least reliable, and a few of the chair's turns absorb a short question from someone else. Several proper nouns are likely misheard. SITLA, the state trust lands agency, appears variously as "Sedla." Lehi is rendered "Lehigh" and Midvale as "Midville." Cory Wride Park appears as "Cory-Ride," "Quarry Ride," "Cordy Wright," and "Cory-Wren." The RAP tax is sometimes "WRAP" or "route tax." At adjournment the chair credits "Jane and Cherie" with seconding, where "Jane" is probably Jay. Names such as Chris Diep, Ty Shepherd, Cam Wixom, Caleb Warnock, and the former mayor referred to as "Gus Morlan" should be verified before quoting. The recreation group referred to as "NOA" or "NOAA" is unclear from audio alone.

docs.text: (see motion text for included items) Charlotte Ducos moved to send City Council a recommended project list including: benches around playgrounds at Smith Ranch Park; trail signage per the trails plan recommendations; ADA roll-up ramps at the recorded locations (with staff reviewing where else they are needed); regular rodeo-grounds maintenance (staff to determine method); commissioning a Nolan Park design through the City's parks design process; working with Firefly to follow up on their offer to build a competition-ready disc golf course; and beginning work with Rocky Mountain Power on the utility-box wildlife art program. Jason Hall (Jay) seconded. The motion passed unanimously. 5. Wrap Tax Funding Criteria The Board discussed the need to create a process and scoring criteria for evaluating projects that apply for wrap-tax funding (e.g., the disc golf proposal). Projects may be recommended by staff, council, nonprofits, or residents, and may involve an application and presentation process. ShaRee Curtis offered to circulate a draft scoring framework to begin from. There is roughly a year before action is required, so detailed criteria were deferred to a future meeting. 6. Sponsorship Policy Implementation — Recreation Signage With the sponsorship policy now adopted, the Board worked through how to solicit sponsors and which fee-schedule additions to recommend. Council's guidance was to avoid an overly commercialized look, so the Board favored a measured “pilot year” and producing a to-scale mock-up (photo of the site with a scaled banner) before bringing it to Council. Direction agreed: • Start with banner sponsorships on the pickleball-court fencing at Cory Park (high visibility from Pony Express / Mid Valley Road and the farmers market), rather than the more labor-intensive soccer-field flags. Soccer is also already getting jersey sponsors. • Target roughly 10 four-by-eight banners placed on the most visible sides (avoiding conflict with the City monument/wayfinding signage and trees), at about $5,000 each for a July 1–June 30 term (potential ~$50,000). • Add a separate, more attainable sponsorship at about $500 covering placement on recreation emails and the website (Junior Jazz / sports registration lists reach several Page 5 of 8 Eagle Mountain Community Services BoardMeeting Minutes thousand families); banner sponsors are also included on the email/website. Consider “gold/silver” tiers or a logo slider. • Consider structuring future fees by sign type (feather flag vs. fence banner) rather than by sport, and prioritize local businesses first (per the existing sign-code tiering). • Funds raised will offset registration costs (e.g., jersey/uniform costs), a scholarship program for kids who cannot afford to register, and coach discounts. Because the core sponsorship policy was already adopted, the fee schedule can be updated via an appendix (likely on the Council consent agenda) without reopening the policy. The Board agreed Chair Southworth will update the fee schedule and prepare a sponsorship flyer (noting the July 1–June 30 term), pending the Board's motion and Jason Hall's agreement as the recreation lead. 7. Community Event Planning Fourth of July Bingo Card Bingo cards are available online, at the farmers market, the library, the front desk, and at events; participants can also photograph themselves and bring it to City Hall or the Chamber for sign-off. Uptake is uncertain so far. Ideas to drive participation: recruit ~6 local influencers to post short videos; emphasize that it should be fun, not just prize-driven. Dawn Hancock offered to dedicate her supply of branded water bottles as prizes. Discussion of prizes included an Eagle Mountain Monopoly board game, backpacks, a commemorative coin/challenge coin, and family picnic/refrigerated bags; the Chamber may help solicit donations (e.g., Walmart) since the Board lacks its own 501(c)(3). America 250 — Backpack Treasure Hunt & Walk 30 Steve Mumford will draft a proposal, timeline, and budget for the backpack treasure hunt and the “Walk 30” challenge and send it to the Board. Backpacks would include a t-shirt, an America-themed pickleball paddle, fanny pack, water bottle, sunglasses, challenge coin, stickers, keychain, and possibly cheap branded preparedness items (flashlight/pocket knife with DTF transfers); golden chocolate coins for those who arrive in time. “Walk 30” would be kept open and creative (e.g., 30 miles, 30 minutes, dogs/family) with its own sticker and existing Walk 30 water bottles. The Board leaned toward launching in August (a more captive audience once school resumes), funded from remaining American 250 funds and carryover into the new fiscal year if donations fall short. Farmers Market booth The Board (Community Services Board booth) agreed to attend the farmers market again to hand out remaining t-shirts and bags and share the bingo-card QR code/stickers, aiming for roughly once a month for visibility. July 11 was selected based on member availability (the market runs until ~1:00 p.m.; setup required by 8:30 a.m., coordinate with John Corrington; remember to bring weights). Other notes Page 6 of 8 Eagle Mountain Community Services BoardMeeting Minutes • Steve Mumford reported a high possibility the Governor could announce a fireworks ban (except for large municipal events); to be confirmed. • Future agendas: the Communications team would like to present on branding and how they can support the Board; “healthy community” items to return next time. 8. Adjournment Outcome: passed unanimously.. Topics: Budget & Finance, Public Works & Infrastructure, Parks & Recreation, Consent Agenda.

docs.title: Forward the Off-Street Trails Master Plan to City Council with a recommendation of approval, in…
docs.text: Forward the Off-Street Trails Master Plan to City Council with a recommendation of approval, in… Charlotte Ducos moved to forward the Off-Street Trails Master Plan to City Council with a recommendation of approval, incorporating: (a) the edits Mr. Mumford has already sent to the consultant; (b) an adjusted (higher) cost estimate for the interpretive signage; and (c) a short-term action item to remediate or remove the hazardous/deteriorating lumber features at the bike park (and any similar hazards identified on City property). Marian Burningham seconded. The motion passed unanimously. 4. Board Priorities and Recommendations The Board reviewed a list of existing and resident-suggested projects to identify priorities to recommend to City Council. Staff noted that personnel capacity — more than funding — is the main constraint, so the Board aimed to recommend a focused, achievable list. Status of current/proposed projects • Observatory (UVU/Astronomy Club, funded in part by Meta): currently planned for Walden Park, but relocating to the Firefly area is being explored for darker skies. Project costs exceed original estimates; county TRCC funding approved, with possible additional City funding. • Festival Field lights: budgeted and being installed to extend evening events. • Cory Park parking lot expansion (west, south of the baseball diamonds): budgeted; in contracting/early work. Page 3 of 8 Eagle Mountain Community Services BoardMeeting Minutes • Ranches Trail on Pony Express: MAG-funded trail through the utility corridor from Pony Express Parkway north to Highway 73; may overlap a proposed disc-golf location. • Soccer fields / field quality: not finalized; options being studied near Cory Park. A new parks technician (Andy, from UVU) is improving existing fields. Water restrictions are in effect; Well #5 is down (motor bearings being repaired, ~2 weeks), reducing field watering. Nolan Park The Board discussed the park's future, including the splash pad (which does not recirculate water; full replacement is estimated near $3 million and is unlikely to reopen as-is), and resident requests for pickleball courts and futsal courts (none currently in the city). Possible locations include the underused baseball area and Nolan Park East. The consensus was that a comprehensive design — rather than piecemeal changes — is the right approach, ideally via a professional design firm that conducts community input as part of its scope. Small wins The Board identified quick, low-cost improvements that demonstrate visible progress: benches at Smith Ranch Park, a requested baby swing, and ADA roll-up ramps. Four ADA ramp locations are already recorded in the City app (concentrated in the Lone Tree area); the Board agreed to start with those and have the Parks Department assess additional needs. Equestrian trails and trail signage Members discussed that many equestrian trails are encroached upon, unmarked, or signed “no trespassing,” and that the City needs a maintenance standard before designating more. The priority identified was trail signage generally (the trails plan includes a dedicated signage funding line), potentially including e-bike regulatory signage. A future equestrian center/rodeo-grounds site in the north should anchor where equestrian trails connect. Rodeo grounds maintenance The arena ground is currently worked only about once a year and is too hard to use safely. The Board favored recommending regular City maintenance (ideally weekly, at least monthly). Jay (Jason) offered to volunteer with City equipment; staff to work out liability and process. Dawn Hancock noted permit fees already exist in the consolidated fee schedule for rodeo-ground use. Disc golf The existing course is poorly located (discs land in backyards) and effectively unusable. Several resident-suggested sites (forwarded by Mac Hampton) were reviewed and largely ruled out due to protected habitat (kestrel/owl areas), private property, or conflicts with bike trails. The Board discussed an offer from Firefly to build a tournament/competition-ready disc golf course (and a dog park) and agreed this option should be pursued. Public art (Wildlife Alliance proposals) Marian Burningham presented arts concepts with rough cost estimates, recommending the quickest, lowest-cost option first: a utility-box wrap art program through Rocky Mountain Power's existing partnership structure (the utility supplies the boxes; the City manages the artist call and Page 4 of 8 Eagle Mountain Community Services BoardMeeting Minutes selection; winning 2-D artwork is printed on vinyl wraps, e.g., ~$400 per design). Roughly 20 boxes were estimated at about $25,300, fitting within the ~$48,000 available in special-revenue (arts) funds. A larger wildlife mural trail concept was estimated near $161,000, with additional ideas (nature center, mural walls, school curriculum, pollinator park) noted for the future. The recommendation is to follow the City's existing public-art approval process and intentionally incorporate wildlife themes, with the Board reviewing designs. Outcome: passed unanimously.. Topics: Public Works & Infrastructure, Parks & Recreation, Personnel & Appointments.

docs.title: Approve the minutes of the previous meeting as presented; ShaRee Curtis seconded. The motion pa…
docs.text: Approve the minutes of the previous meeting as presented; ShaRee Curtis seconded. The motion pa… Charlotte Ducos moved to approve the minutes of the previous meeting as presented; ShaRee Curtis seconded. The motion passed unanimously (all in favor). 2. Recap from the Previous Meeting The Chair reviewed items advanced since the last meeting: Page 1 of 8 Eagle Mountain Community Services BoardMeeting Minutes • The Board's rules of order were passed by City Council. • A new sponsorship policy was passed by City Council. • The City received approval for a municipal recreation grant for a trail/path project (see Item 3). • The Fourth of July bingo card was completed and is being promoted by the Communications Department, with thanks to Charlotte Ducos, Melissa Clark, and staff. Communications posted it with the Fourth of July festivities and will push it again on social media; members were asked to repost. GRANT NOTE: Steve Mumford explained the approved grant funds a path just east of Walden Park, pushed as far north as practical through the open-space area so it ties into the existing Walden Park path and preserves room for future improvements. The grant is essentially guaranteed; the City must identify funds to cover the (potentially significant) cost difference. 3. Off-Street Trails Master Plan Steve Mumford presented the draft Off-Street Trails Master Plan, funded by a UDOT planning-assistance grant and prepared by consultant Bike Utah. Originally managed by the late Todd Black, the project was carried to completion by Mr. Mumford. The plan intentionally addresses biking, hiking, equestrian, and OHV use, though most existing trails are mountain-bike oriented. Key elements of the plan: • A trail network assessment covering every existing trail, noting land-ownership, development, and environmental conflicts, signage needs, erosion, slope/width issues, hazards, and undesirable “social trails.” Usage data was drawn from the Trailforks and Strava apps; equestrian data is limited. • Trail areas include Upper Hidden Valley (highest use; e.g., Deadwood Trail ~6,000 users), the Southern Trails along the eastern foothills, the Mountain Ranch Bike Park (power corridor), and newer Firefly trails. • Mountain Ranch Bike Park: a consultant (Shape Shift Terrains) proposed a redesign to serve beginner/intermediate riders, relocate and improve the jump line, and add a skills area and drop zone. Many resident-built wooden features are deteriorating and present a liability concern. • Eagle Mountain NICA (high-school) race course: development conflicts mean it likely cannot remain in Upper Hidden Valley; relocation to BLM property or the Firefly area is recommended. • Trailheads and signage: consistent trailhead, directional, regulatory, etiquette, and interpretive signage is recommended, with Lake Mountain Trails Association and SITLA logos where applicable. Page 2 of 8 Eagle Mountain Community Services BoardMeeting Minutes • Land access: Mr. Mumford is pursuing an MOU with SITLA (with the Lake Mountain Trails Association) for legal trail access, preserving development rights while keeping a connected system; private landowners to follow. Cost ranges noted: Mountain Ranch Bike Park improvements roughly $1–$1.5 million; trailhead and trail signage roughly $262,000–$586,000. Marian Burningham noted the interpretive-sign estimate appears too low based on the Wildlife Alliance's recent Nature Park signs and offered to share actual vendor costs. No funding has been set aside specifically for this plan; it is a phased recommendation, not a commitment to immediate spending. Discussion points: • Dawn Hancock noted a finalized SITLA/landowner access agreement could simplify the special-event permit packet for bike clubs. • The Board agreed the deteriorating wooden bike-park features are a significant liability and should be removed or remediated in the short term (within a couple of months), potentially as a volunteer project with the Lake Mountain Trails Association and/or corporate volunteer groups. • Next steps: present the plan to City Council in a work session (targeted for July 7), then return for adoption. The plan recommends a Trails Advisory Committee; absent one, the Community Services Board would serve in that role. Outcome: passed unanimously (all in favor).. Topics: Public Works & Infrastructure, Parks & Recreation, Contracts & Procurement.

docs.title: Every property tax on an Eagle Mountain bill — 2025 rates
docs.text: Every property tax levied on an Eagle Mountain parcel, not just the city's. These are the 2025 final adopted rates for Utah County tax area 038-0000, which covers most of the city, and they total 0.009377. 7 taxing entities appear on the bill and the City Council sets exactly one of them. Alpine School District: rate 0.005774 (61.6% of the bill) — Public schools — the district Eagle Mountain's schools belong to. The largest single line on the bill by a wide margin. Unified Fire Service Area: rate 0.001650 (17.6% of the bill) — Fire and emergency medical response. Eagle Mountain sits inside this service area, so the fire levy is charged on the bill directly rather than out of the city's own rate. Utah County: rate 0.000893 (9.5% of the bill) — County government — the jail, the courts, elections, county roads, and the Sheriff's Office county-wide. Eagle Mountain's own contract with the Sheriff is paid by the city, out of the city's line below. Eagle Mountain City: rate 0.000534 (5.7% of the bill) — The city's own general levy — the one line on this bill the City Council sets, and the one the estimator above is about. Central Utah Water Conservancy District: rate 0.000400 (4.3% of the bill) — Wholesale water — the district that develops and delivers Central Utah Project water to cities along the Wasatch Front. County Assessing & Collecting Levy: rate 0.000112 (1.2% of the bill) — Pays Utah County to value property and collect the tax — the assessor, recorder, and treasurer's side of the bill. Multicounty Assessing & Collecting Levy: rate 0.000014 (0.1% of the bill) — A statewide levy set in state law, not by any local board, that funds property valuation standards across all 29 counties. The smallest line on the bill. Rates are the 2025 final adopted figures — the ones on bills mailed in 2025. The 2026 rates for the county, the school district, the water district and the fire service area are set on their own schedules and are not final yet; only Eagle Mountain's 2026 rate is settled, adopted by its council on August 18 — 0.000900, replacing the 0.001500 it adopted on August 6 and repealed that night. Of the six, only Central Utah Water has noticed an increase for 2026, of 0.76% — about a dollar a year on an average home. This is the picture for the tax area covering most of Eagle Mountain. Your own parcel's tax area is printed on your valuation notice, and three areas add a local district on top of these seven levies. Property tax is not the whole bill. City utility charges, garbage, and stormwater fees are billed separately and are not property taxes. A primary residence is taxed on 55% of its market value. Every entity in the table levies against that same reduced value, so the exemption applies to all of them at once.
