docs.title: How the rate compares — Utah County cities, 2025 rates
docs.text: How Eagle Mountain's city property tax rate compares with other cities. These are 2025 final adopted municipal rates — the city's own levy only, not the county, school district or special districts. Eagle Mountain's 0.000534 is the 2nd-lowest of the 26 cities in Utah County, against a county median of 0.001032. The adopted 0.000900 makes it the 20th-highest, once every other city's own proposed increase is applied. Rates today, highest to lowest: Vineyard 0.003796, Woodland Hills 0.003093, Provo 0.001678, American Fork 0.001532, Mapleton 0.001456, Santaquin 0.001409, Payson 0.001299, Alpine 0.001201, Pleasant Grove 0.001179, Lehi 0.001163, Salem 0.001144, Springville 0.001079, Cedar Hills 0.001043, Elk Ridge 0.001020, Spanish Fork 0.000986, Saratoga Springs 0.000976, Goshen 0.000957, Genola 0.000949, Draper 0.000936, Bluffdale 0.000866, Lindon 0.000788, Orem 0.000755, Highland 0.000740, Fairfield 0.000655, Eagle Mountain 0.000534, Cedar Fort 0.000457. 8 Utah County cities noticed a 2026 increase. Eagle Mountain: +69.81% for Sheriff's deputies / public safety, about $99 a year on a $488,000 home. Saratoga Springs: +50.03% for Fire and police services, about $146 a year on a $542,000 home. Cedar Hills: +19.55% for Public safety contracts, about $54 a year on a $682,000 home. Pleasant Grove: +8.72% for Two police, three firefighters, about $27 a year on a $602,000 home. American Fork: +8.48% for Nine full-time firefighters, about $33 a year on a $502,000 home. Orem: +6.95% for Two new police officers (Public-safety levy, not the general city rate), about $12 a year on a $520,000 home. Highland: +6.89% for Library staffing (Library levy, not the general city rate), about $28 a year on a $1,036,000 home. Springville: +2.97% for Offset inflation costs, about $6 a year on a $476,000 home. Statewide, of all 253 Utah cities, Eagle Mountain's current rate is the 64th-lowest; the adopted rate is the 132nd-highest, measuring it against every other city's current rate — the state does not publish a full set of 2026 proposals. The same page carries a second comparison against the 23 cities of Salt Lake County, where Eagle Mountain is shown as an out-of-county reference: its current rate would be the 9th-lowest there, and the adopted rate the 14th-highest once each of those cities' own increases is applied. Current rates are 2025 final adopted rates — the newest complete set the state publishes. 2026 rates are not certified until after the August hearings. Eagle Mountain is the one city here whose 2026 rate is settled, and it took two votes to settle it: the council adopted 0.001500 on August 6 after noticing 0.001700 and hearing nearly three hours of public comment, then repealed that rate on August 18 and adopted 0.000900 in its place. The charts carry the adopted 0.000900 for Eagle Mountain and each other city's noticed figure for the rest, whose hearings run through late August. Eagle Mountain's tentative schedule (read May 26) implied a rate of 0.001842 and a 245% increase. The rate it noticed was 0.001700, which its notice states as 220.88% — the rise in budgeted revenue excluding eligible new growth. Measured as a ratio of rates instead, 0.001700 against the 0.000530 certified rate is 220.75%. The rate it first adopted was 0.001500, a 183.02% increase; the rate in force is the 0.000900 adopted on August 18, which is 69.81% over the certified rate. Both of those come out the same on either basis, which the noticed figure does not. Percent increases are each entity's own noticed figure, exactly as Utah County advertised it: the rise in that entity's property tax budgeted revenue, excluding eligible new growth. They are not increases in your total tax bill, and they are not the ratio of proposed collections to current collections — for Eagle Mountain the adopted rate's ratio is 204.5%, against the 183.02% in the motion. Every proposal charted here is read off Utah County's combined notice, linked below, rather than off press coverage. Two cities a July news summary listed as proposing increases — Lehi and Santaquin — appear neither on the county's advertised notice nor on the Utah Taxpayers Association's statewide compilation of every 2026 notice, so they are not charted. Draper is on the county notice at 22.55% but is not charted here, being mostly a Salt Lake County city; its Salt Lake County proposal is on the other tab. Provo City School District and the Central Utah Water Conservancy District are on the notice but are not cities. Eagle Mountain's line matches this page to the dollar: $142.25 to $456.28 on a $488,000 home, $6,742,938, 220.88%. Highland's and Orem's proposals raise a dedicated levy (library; public safety) rather than the general city rate, but the percentage and the dollar figures shown for them are the entity-wide ones the county notice states — the same basis as every other row. Draper and Bluffdale levy in Utah County but lie mostly in Salt Lake County. Resulting rates are each city's current rate plus the rate increase implied by its own noticed figures (the dollar rise on its stated average home, over 55% of that home's value). This avoids assuming the noticed percentage applies to the general city rate — for Highland and Orem it does not. The notice's ‘from’ column is each entity's 2026 certified rate rather than its 2025 adopted rate, so the sum is close rather than exact: on Eagle Mountain — the one city that published a proposed rate — the method gives 0.001704 against the 0.001700 it noticed. The 0.000900 in the charts is the rate it went on to adopt on August 18 — read off the council's decision rather than derived, as was the 0.001500 it adopted on August 6 and repealed.

docs.title: Road fees on the utility bill — Utah County cities that charge one
docs.text: Transportation utility fees — road fees charged on the monthly city utility bill, not through the property tax. 4 Utah County cities charge one, so a comparison of property tax rates understates what a household there pays for streets. A fee is set by resolution and is not subject to Truth-in-Taxation notices or hearings, and it is flat: the same on every home, whatever it is worth. Residential rates as of 2026-08-03: Highland: $18.50 a month, $222.00 a year — the same as a property tax rate of 0.000807 on a $500,000 home. Adopted May 2017 after a study found 45% of city roads poor or failing; scheduled to end June 30, 2028, when the road bonds are paid off. Mapleton: $8.00 a month, $96.00 a year — the same as a property tax rate of 0.000349 on a $500,000 home. City code establishes a utility road fund paid by utility users; the amount is set in the consolidated utility fee schedule. Pleasant Grove: $6.76 a month, $81.12 a year — the same as a property tax rate of 0.000295 on a $500,000 home. Charged by intensity of street use: $6.76 residential, $33.02 and $188.84 for the two commercial tiers. Challenged in court and upheld as a fee, not a tax, in Larson v. Pleasant Grove City (2023 UT 2). Provo: $4.20 a month, $50.40 a year — the same as a property tax rate of 0.000183 on a $500,000 home. Residential A (single family) rate; billed on the monthly consolidated utility bill under Provo City Code 5.08. Eagle Mountain charges no such fee. Eagle Mountain's consolidated fee schedule carries no road or transportation charge on a residential utility bill. Its residential utility fees are water, sewer, storm drain and garbage. For scale, Eagle Mountain's entire city property tax on a $500,000 primary residence is $146.85 a year today. The fee is flat. Every household pays the same, whatever the home is worth, so it lands hardest on the least valuable homes — the opposite of how a property tax rate works. The rate equivalents are what each fee would cost as a property tax rate on a $500,000 primary residence, taxed on 55% of value. They are for scale only; no city levies these as a rate. A fee is not a tax. It is set by resolution and is not subject to Truth-in-Taxation notices or hearings, which is part of why cities use it. Utah's Supreme Court upheld Pleasant Grove's as a fee rather than a tax in 2023, remanding on whether the amount was reasonable. About a dozen Utah cities charge one; these four are the Utah County cities identified in a March 2026 survey and confirmed against each city's current fee schedule. A city that adopted one since would not appear here.

docs.title: Every tax increase proposed in Utah — 2026 truth-in-taxation notices
docs.text: Every 2026 truth-in-taxation notice in Utah, not just Eagle Mountain's and not just cities. 79 notices from 68 taxing entities in 18 counties — cities, towns, school districts, water conservancy districts and fire districts — asking for $96,055,660 between them, with hearings from 2026-08-03 to 2026-08-27. Eagle Mountain's is the only settled figure on the list: its council adopted 0.000900 on 2026-08-18, an increase of 69.81%. Measured against every other entity's noticed figure that is the 8th-steepest increase in the state, the 19th-heaviest on an average home at $99.31 a year, and the 10th-largest by revenue at $2,132,876. Every other entity's hearing may still land lower than its notice. The fifteen steepest proposals in Utah: Ogden Valley City (Weber County, city) +512.61%, no rate published, $555.32 a year on a $1,222,000 home, $2,475,138 raised, hearing 2026-08-11; Boulder Town (Garfield County, town) +185.23%, levy 0.000176 to 0.000502, $53.79 a year on a $300,000 home, $12,897 raised, hearing 2026-08-11; Hildale City (Washington County, city) +167.91%, levy 0.001072 to 0.002872, $448.47 a year on a $453,000 home, $210,219 raised, hearing 2026-08-05; Nephi City (Juab County, city) +109.13%, levy 0.000493 to 0.001031, $132.56 a year on a $448,000 home, $523,000 raised, hearing 2026-08-11; Fielding Town (Box Elder County, town) +85.93%, levy 0.000334 to 0.000621, $71.03 a year on a $450,000 home, $13,868 raised, hearing 2026-08-12; Deweyville Town (Box Elder County, town) +79.43%, levy 0.000705 to 0.001265, $149.38 a year on a $485,000 home, $32,000 raised, hearing 2026-08-20; River Heights City (Cache County, city) +73.27%, levy 0.000490 to 0.000849, $104.85 a year on a $531,000 home, $85,101 raised, hearing 2026-08-17; Eagle Mountain City (Utah County, city) +69.81%, levy 0.000530 to 0.000900, $99.31 a year on a $488,000 home, $2,132,876 raised, adopted 2026-08-06; Roy City (Weber County, city) +54.98%, levy 0.001608 to 0.002492, $213.44 a year on a $439,000 home, $2,807,745 raised, hearing 2026-08-11; Castle Valley Town (Grand County, town) +54.13%, levy 0.000774 to 0.001193, $105.78 a year on a $459,000 home, $73,666 raised, hearing 2026-08-12; Saratoga Springs City (Utah County, city) +50.0%, levy 0.000978 to 0.001467, $145.77 a year on a $542,000 home, $3,100,000 raised, hearing 2026-08-11; Woods Cross City (Davis County, city) +46.84%, levy 0.001298 to 0.001906, $181.58 a year on a $543,000 home, $995,285 raised, hearing 2026-08-04; Hooper City (Weber County, city) +46.57%, levy 0.000277 to 0.000406, $44.70 a year on a $630,000 home, $128,000 raised, hearing 2026-08-06; Cottonwood Heights City (Salt Lake County, city) +36.31%, levy 0.001468 to 0.002001, $249.18 a year on a $850,000 home, $3,454,767 raised, hearing 2026-08-11; Richfield City (Sevier County, city) +32.31%, levy 0.001721 to 0.002277, $100.91 a year on a $330,000 home, $500,000 raised, hearing 2026-08-11. Every percentage here is the increase over that entity's own certified rate — the rate that would raise the same money as last year. It is not an increase in anyone's total tax bill: a city, a school district, a water district and sometimes a fire district all levy on the same parcel, and only one of them is on this list. The dollar figure is the effect on an average home in that entity, and each entity picked its own average. They run from $300,000 in Boulder to $1,895,000 in Summit County's slice of the Weber Basin district, so the dollar column compares typical households, not identical ones. 79 notices, 68 entities: Central Utah Water Conservancy District notices in seven counties, Weber Basin in five, and Draper in two, each with its own hearing and its own figures. Ranking by revenue counts each notice separately, so those entities' totals are split across rows. The Utah Taxpayers Association's own headline — 67 entities, $93,580,522 — leaves out Ogden Valley City, which incorporated too recently to have a certified rate and shows ‘Not Available’ in both rate columns. Its $2,475,138 is included in the $96.1M total here, and it is ranked on the 512.61% its notice states. Six rows have been corrected against the counties' own notices, and are marked † in the table. The Association's dollar column is derived — an entity's taxable value times the gap between its two rate columns — so where a rate column is wrong or missing, the dollars are too. Cedar Hills, Orem, Springville, Pleasant Grove and American Fork carried a proposed rate above the one Utah County advertised, which put their percentages and dollar figures roughly two to fifteen times too high; each is now read off the county's combined notice. Ogden Valley, having no certified rate to subtract, carried its whole proposed tax bill in the increase column; it now carries the increase its own impact schedule states. No revenue figure changed, and every correction moved a row down. None of it disturbs Eagle Mountain's position: the five Utah County rows sit well below it on every measure either way, and Ogden Valley stays above it on percentage and on the average home, as it was. Eagle Mountain's row is the rate its council adopted on August 18, replacing the 0.001500 it adopted on August 6 and repealed the same night — the one row here that is a decision rather than a proposal, and the one that has already shown a council can move a long way between the two. Every other row is that entity's noticed figure, and a hearing can end in a smaller increase than the one noticed, or in none at all — Eagle Mountain's did, after nearly three hours of public comment. So the ranking compares one settled rate against seventy-eight opening asks, and several of those will come down.

docs.title: The rate the council adopted — 0.000900, 2026-08-18
docs.text: What Eagle Mountain's City Council actually adopted. On 2026-08-18 the council voted to set the city property tax rate at 0.000900 — not the 0.001700 on the public notice. That is an increase of 69.81% over the 0.000530 certified rate, rather than the 220.75% noticed. It adds about $99.31 a year to a $488,000 primary residence, instead of $314.03, and raises roughly $2,132,876 rather than $6,742,938. The money goes to the Utah County Sheriff's contract and the deputies it funds. It replaced 0.001500, which the same council adopted on 2026-08-06 — 183.02% over the certified rate, about $260.35 a year on the same home — and repealed on 2026-08-18 before any bill was issued. The resolution, the vote and the motion had not been published when this was written, so every figure here except the rate itself is derived from the rate. Source: City Council meeting, August 18, 2026 — budget adoption, items 13.A and 13.B. The rate is the council's; every other figure in this row is derived from it, because the adopting resolution and the recording were not yet published when it was written. The $2,132,876 is the certified rate's own $3,055,201 scaled by 0.000900 ÷ 0.000530, less that $3,055,201; the 69.81% is the same ratio as a percentage, and comes out identical whether it is read as a ratio of rates or of revenue. The $99.31 is this list's own arithmetic, the one it applies to every row: an average home's taxable value — $268,400, being 55% of the $488,000 on the city's notice — times the 0.000370 the rate rose over the certified rate.

docs.title: How many people work for Eagle Mountain — FY2024
docs.text: Eagle Mountain City employed 146.58 full-time equivalents in FY2024, for a Census-estimated 61,362 residents — 2.389 per 1,000. The city employs nobody in police or fire: patrol is contracted from the Utah County Sheriff's Office (Eagle Mountain Division) and fire and ambulance come from Unified Fire Authority, so the 4.82 FTE it reports under public safety are crossing guards. By function: General government 30.27, Planning & development 21.75, Streets & public works 24.35, Police, fire & emergency 4.82, Parks & recreation 22.38, Library 10.25, Utilities 32.76. In 2014 the city had 84.35 FTE for 25,919 residents, so headcount has grown more slowly than population. Separately, the city's HR director told the Council in May 2026 that the city then had 236 employees against fewer than 100 full-time in 2019 — that is a headcount including part-time staff two years later, not the same measure as full-time equivalents.

docs.title: Is Eagle Mountain a third the size of comparable cities?
docs.text: The city manager told the Council in August 2026 that Eagle Mountain's staff is about a third the size of cities of equivalent population. Checked against the audited FTE schedules of the Utah cities nearest Eagle Mountain in population, the answer depends on whether contracted services are counted. On raw headcount Eagle Mountain is 36% of the peer median (2.389 per 1,000 against 6.643) — the leanest city in the set, and the claim is about right. Excluding police and fire on every city's side, which is the like-for-like comparison because Eagle Mountain contracts both, it is 64% of the median (2.31 against 3.63) — nearer two thirds than one third. Excluding utilities as well it is 65%. So the claim is true of the headcount and overstated as a measure of how thinly the city is staffed: most of the gap is that other cities employ their own police and firefighters. Peers, per 1,000 residents: Murray 7.775 raw and 4.759 excluding police and fire, Logan 7.649 raw and 4.834 excluding police and fire, American Fork 7.111 raw and 3.71 excluding police and fire, Draper 6.176 raw and 3.549 excluding police and fire, Riverton 3.554 raw and 2.537 excluding police and fire, Herriman 3.181 raw and 2.214 excluding police and fire.

docs.title: The council raised your property taxes 220 percent.
docs.text: Claim in circulation: “The council raised your property taxes 220 percent.” Verdict: Overtaken by events. 220.88% was noticed in June and never adopted. The rate that survives is 0.000900 — 69.81% over the certified rate, on the city's own line, which is about a twentieth of a property tax bill. What is true: The number was real and the city printed it. The Truth-in-Taxation notice mailed in June proposed 0.001700 against a 0.000530 certified rate and stated the increase as 220.88% — a rise in the city's budgeted property tax revenue over the prior year, excluding eligible new growth. Where it goes wrong: Two things. The figure is three rates out of date: the council adopted 0.001500 on August 6, repealed it on August 18, and adopted 0.000900 in its place. And it was never a percentage of anybody's tax bill — it is a percentage of the city's own levy, which is one of seven lines on an Eagle Mountain bill and the fourth-largest of them. On the notice's own average home — $488,000 of market value, $268,400 taxable after Utah's 55% primary-residence exemption — the noticed rate would have added $314.03 a year. The rate in force adds $99.31. On that same home the city's line goes from about $143 a year to about $242, inside a total bill of about $2,517 at 2025 rates. That is the city's share moving from roughly 5.7% of the bill to roughly 9.2% of it. Alpine School District's line alone is more than six times the city's. Noticed, June: 0.001700 (+220.88% · never adopted). Adopted 6 August: 0.001500 (+183.02% · repealed 12 days later). In force: 0.000900 (+69.81% over the certified rate). Average home: +$99.31 a year (was $314.03 as noticed). Still provisional: The 0.000900 is certain; the vote, the motion and the figures the adopting resolution recites were not published when this was written, so everything priced at that rate here is this project's arithmetic on it. Mayor Jared Gray, reading the impact schedule on 2026-06-16, meeting #726: “Eagle Mountain City will consider an increase to its property tax rate to generate an additional $6,958,141… Eagle Mountain City's current property tax rate is 0.000534… The estimated increase to Eagle Mountain City's property tax revenue is 218%… The affected budget is the Sheriff contract.” The repeal and re-adoption on 2026-08-18, meeting #728: Two resolutions taken in order: one repealing the increase approved on August 6, one approving an increase above the certified rate in its place at 0.000900. Last checked 2026-08-19.

docs.title: Every dollar of the increase goes straight to public safety.
docs.text: Claim in circulation: “Every dollar of the increase goes straight to public safety.” Verdict: Accurate, but incomplete. True in the schedule's own terms — the levy is smaller than the Sheriff's contract, so there is no second dollar to allocate. What it left out is that the money largely replaces sales tax already paying that contract, and frees the sales tax for other things. The city's own claim, not one aimed at it. What is true: The statutory impact schedule names the Sheriff's contract as the affected budget and puts it at $9,798,139 — the same figure, to the dollar, as the proposed property tax revenue. Designed that way, the levy covers the contract and nothing else. Where it goes wrong: What actually changes is which pot pays. Property tax takes over a contract sales tax had been subsidising, and the freed sales tax goes to other city spending — parks, roads, staff. That is a defensible policy and it is not what "every dollar goes to public safety" conveys, which is why residents who did the subtraction — $6.74 million noticed against a $1.5 million rise in the contract — concluded they had been lied to. At the rate finally adopted the gap runs the other way and is larger. 0.000900 raises about $5.19 million against a contract of $9,798,139, so roughly $4.61 million of the Sheriff's contract still comes out of sales tax — four times what the repealed rate would have left short. Sheriff's contract: $9,798,139 (the affected budget on the schedule). Rise in the contract: $1,507,939 (over the no-change budget). Raised at 0.000900: ≈$5.19M (leaving ≈$4.61M on sales tax). Mayor Jared Gray, reading the schedule on 2026-08-06, meeting #747: “The affected budget, sheriff's contract. The proposed budget is $9,798,139. The budget with no tax change is $8,290,000, and the budget change would be $1,507,939.” Councilmember Craig Whiting on 2026-08-06, meeting #747: “When we say that 100% of the property tax increase goes to public safety, that is the correct answer. What we need to do is help you understand — and this means we didn't communicate this well enough — how public safety has been paid… we're essentially robbing from sales tax to help subsidize our police.” Duncan Searcy, resident, quoting the city on 2026-08-06, meeting #747: “Eagle Mountain City is proposing a property tax increase with every dollar going straight to public safety, period. So that's a lie, and we all know that now.” Last checked 2026-08-19.

docs.title: City staff is about a third the size of a city our size.
docs.text: Claim in circulation: “City staff is about a third the size of a city our size.” Verdict: Misleading. Right on raw headcount — 36% of the median of comparable Utah cities — but most of that gap is that those cities employ their own police and firefighters and Eagle Mountain contracts both. Compared like for like it is 64%, nearer two thirds than one third. The city manager's claim, made at the August 6 hearing. What is true: On raw headcount the claim is about right, and the underlying point stands: Eagle Mountain is the leanest city in the comparison set. It employed 146.58 full-time equivalents in FY2024 for about 61,400 residents — 2.389 per 1,000, against a peer median of 6.643. Where it goes wrong: The comparison counts other cities' police officers and firefighters and cannot count Eagle Mountain's, because Eagle Mountain has none to count. Set public safety aside on every city's side and the ratio is 2.31 against 3.63 per 1,000 — 64% of the median. Set utilities aside too and it is 65%. So the sentence is true of the payroll and overstated as a measure of how thinly the city is run. Both halves matter: a resident hearing "a third the size" is being told the city is stretched three times thinner than its neighbours, and on the work the city actually does itself the honest figure is about a third thinner. Raw headcount: 36% (2.389 per 1,000 against a 6.643 median). Excluding police and fire: 64% (2.31 against 3.63 — the like-for-like figure). City employees: 146.58 FTE (FY2024, for about 61,400 residents). City Manager Ben Reeves on 2026-08-06, meeting #747: “Our city staff is about the third of the size of city staff of equivalent population, and they are working their hearts out… I truly feel like for many, many years that they've been working with basically an arm tied behind their back. We haven't invested in them.” Audited headcount, eight Utah cities on 2026-08-18: Every figure is the GASB 44 full-time-equivalent schedule in each city's own annual financial report, compared against Census population for the same year. Last checked 2026-08-19.

docs.title: They did this in secret and rushed it through.
docs.text: Claim in circulation: “They did this in secret and rushed it through.” Verdict: Unsupported by the record. Two different charges are tangled together. On whether it was done in the open the record is unusually complete — seven open meetings from April 14, both August hearings set three months ahead, the schedule read into the record four times. On whether residents found out, the council agrees with the criticism: four of five said so from the dais before voting. What is true: Residents did not hear about it in time to weigh in early, and that is not in dispute. The council conceded it on the record before the vote, and the concession is the strongest evidence for the complaint. Where it goes wrong: Nothing was done outside a noticed public meeting. The Sheriff's Office presented the staffing case in an open work session on April 14; on May 5 the council accepted the tentative budget, acknowledged the proposed increase and declared its intent to exceed the certified rate, setting both August hearings; the impact schedule was read on May 26, June 2 and June 16, and the June 16 hearing ran with public comment answered at length. The August 6 hearing took about sixty speakers over three hours. Open meetings: 7 (April 14 to August 6, before the first adoption). Schedule read: 4 times (May 26, June 2, June 16, August 6). Hearings set: 3 months ahead (both fixed by resolution on May 5). Councilmember Zac Huish on 2026-08-06, meeting #747: “Transparency — we failed you. We absolutely failed you.” Councilmember Rich Wood on 2026-08-06, meeting #747: “I think we did a horrible job of communication. I think that's been highlighted by every person here. And so for that, I want to apologize… I will own that. I should have communicated.” Three resolutions in one night on 2026-05-05, meeting #712: Tentative budget accepted, the Budget Officer's statement of a proposed increase acknowledged, and intent to exceed the certified rate declared — which is what fixed both August hearing dates. Last checked 2026-08-19.

docs.title: The increase pays for the city's own police department.
docs.text: Claim in circulation: “The increase pays for the city's own police department.” Verdict: Not accurate. Eagle Mountain employs no police officers and no firefighters. Patrol is bought from the Utah County Sheriff's Office; fire and ambulance come from Unified Fire Authority, which bills residents on a separate line of the same tax notice. What is true: The money does pay for policing. The affected budget on the impact schedule is the Sheriff's contract, and the deputies it funds are assigned to the Eagle Mountain division. Where it goes wrong: It is a contract, not a department. The city's audited schedule shows 4.82 full-time equivalents under public safety and every one of them is a crossing guard; the line for firefighters and officers reads zero, and has read zero for eleven years. Fire and ambulance are not the city's at all — Unified Fire Service Area levies 0.001650 directly, which is nearly twice the city's own new rate. This matters for reading a tax bill. Someone comparing Eagle Mountain's rate against a neighbouring city that runs its own police and fire is comparing a city that buys those services against one that levies for them, and the neighbour's higher rate is partly that difference. City police officers: 0 (patrol contracted from the county Sheriff). City firefighters: 0 (Unified Fire Authority, on its own levy). City "public safety" staff: 4.82 FTE (crossing guards). The city's own audited staffing schedule on 2026-08-18: The ten-year full-time-equivalent table in the city's annual financial report: public safety 4.82, firefighters and officers 0.00. Utah State Tax Commission, Report 600 on 2026-01-05: The seven levies on an Eagle Mountain bill, including Unified Fire Service Area at 0.001650 and the city at 0.000534 for 2025. Last checked 2026-08-19.

docs.title: Sign the petition and the tax goes away.
docs.text: Claim in circulation: “Sign the petition and the tax goes away.” Verdict: Not settled. A referendum on a property tax rate is legally available, and one ran in a Utah city as recently as last autumn. But the resolution a petition was organised against was repealed on August 18 and replaced, and the signature test is two thresholds rather than one. What is true: Utah Code § 20A-7-613 exists for exactly this situation. Five sponsors file a notarised application with the resolution attached; the city's budget officer must then produce an unbiased fiscal and legal impact statement within days; then signatures are gathered against a statutory threshold. Where it goes wrong: Nothing about it is automatic, and two things are genuinely unsettled. The first is what a petition aimed at the August 6 resolution does now that the resolution has been repealed and a smaller increase adopted in its place — that turns on what was filed and when, and the city recorder is the authority on it, not this page. The second is the threshold itself. For a city of the second class it is 8.25% of active voters citywide and 8.25% within at least 75% of the city's voter participation areas. Both must be met, and the second is what decides these — it is the one almost nobody organising a petition budgets for. Whether Eagle Mountain is second class yet is itself open. The statutory line is 65,000 residents, the first statewide subcounty estimates put the city at 65,409 in 2025, and the class changes on the lieutenant governor's certificate rather than on the estimate. If that certificate has not issued, the thresholds are 10% rather than 8.25%. Citywide signatures: 8.25% (of active voters — 10% if still third class). And by area: 75% (of voter participation areas must each clear 8.25%). Utah Code on 2026-08-19: § 20A-7-601 (thresholds and filing deadline), § 20A-7-602.5 (the city's impact statement), § 20A-7-613 (referendum on a tax), § 10-2-301 and § 67-1a-2(3)(d) (city class, and the certificate that changes it). Last checked 2026-08-19.

docs.title: They're building another data center in Eagle Mountain.
docs.text: Claim in circulation: “They're building another data center in Eagle Mountain.” Verdict: Accurate. Yes, and the votes are on file. What is being built is more of what is already here — every data center approval in the record since 2024 is an expansion by Meta or QTS, not a new company arriving. What is true: Three campuses are already named in the city's own record — Meta, Google and QTS — and building has not stopped. QTS's SLC1 site was still under construction this spring, when the council let it work outside the hours city code normally allows. A second QTS parcel, the land the motion calls QTS-SCL 2, was rezoned on March 3. And on October 21 the council approved a development agreement with Stadion, LLC, the company known as Meta, on a 4–1 vote, along with a third amendment to its water and sewer agreement the same night. Where it goes wrong: “Another” suggests a new operator. Nothing in the record shows one. It is also worth knowing what has not happened yet: the newest land in play — the parcel west of the Pony Express area that QTS has bought — was described to the council on August 4 as still zoned agricultural. Farmland cannot be built on until the council rezones it, and a rezone is a public vote with a public hearing in front of it. The scale of it gets overstated in both directions. A resident told the council in February that they had read five more had been approved. In the twelve months before that comment the council passed four measures touching the data centers — a road realignment at the Meta site, the Meta development agreement, the water and sewer amendment beside it, and a sign-code rule for directional signage — and none of the four approved a new data center. The motions themselves are thin, which is a fair complaint about the record rather than about the claim. The QTS-SCL 2 rezone does not state the acreage or the new zoning, and the Meta development agreement does not list its terms. The votes are public; what was voted on is often summarised in a single line. Operators on file: 3 (Meta, Google and QTS). QTS-SCL 2 rezoned: 3 Mar 2026 (acreage and new zoning not stated in the motion). Meta agreement: 4–1 (21 Oct 2025, with Stadion, LLC). Rezone the land known as QTS-SCL 2 on 2026-03-03, vote #1046: Passed unanimously. The motion does not state the acreage or the new zoning. Longer construction hours at the QTS SLC1 site on 2026-03-25, vote #1055: Passed 4–0 — the site was under construction this spring. Development agreement with Stadion, LLC, the company known as Meta on 2025-10-21, vote #972: Passed 4–1, the only split vote among these. A business owner, addressing the council on 2026-08-04, meeting #715: “We've also learned that QTS, of course, bought the property to the west, which is zoned agricultural now but could also go industrial.” Last checked 2026-08-19.

docs.title: It's going to be the largest data center in the country, maybe the world.
docs.text: Claim in circulation: “It's going to be the largest data center in the country, maybe the world.” Verdict: Not accurate. No. A single project already approved in Box Elder County covers 40,000 acres — more ground than the whole of Eagle Mountain, which is 32,256 acres of land. Whatever gets built here, the largest in the country is not going in this city. What is true: The premise underneath it is sound. Eagle Mountain has three data center campuses, it keeps approving work on them, and QTS has bought more ground west of the Pony Express area that has not been through the council yet. Somebody hearing that a company is buying more land here is hearing something true, and the state as a whole genuinely is getting enormous ones. Where it goes wrong: It is the superlative that fails, and it fails on a comparison anyone can make. The Stratos project area in western Box Elder County — a data and energy campus approved by the MIDA board on April 24 and agreed to by the Box Elder County Commission on May 4 — covers 40,000 acres. Eagle Mountain City is 50.4 square miles of land, which is 32,256 acres. The project area 200 miles north is about a quarter larger than this entire city, and it is the one Utah newsrooms have been calling the largest in the country. Two honest qualifications, neither of which rescues the claim. The 40,000 acres is the project area rather than the buildings: the state's own FAQ says most of it will stay undeveloped and the data center footprint will be “a fraction” of it. And those April and May votes created the project area, not the project — the state says plainly that they did not approve the full development, which still needs air, water and wildlife review. The other half of the problem is local, and it is the more useful half. Nothing Eagle Mountain has voted on states a size for anything. The QTS-SCL 2 rezone does not give the acreage or the zoning it granted; the Meta development agreement does not list its terms. So there is no figure in the city's record that a claim about size could be measured against — which is exactly why a superlative can circulate here for weeks without meeting a number. Stratos project area: 40,000 acres (Box Elder County, approved April–May 2026). All of Eagle Mountain: 32,256 acres (50.4 sq mi of land, US Census). Size stated locally: None (no acreage or footprint in any Eagle Mountain motion). Utah Governor's Office, on the Stratos Project Area on 2026-05-04: “While the entire project area encompasses 40,000 acres, most of the acres will remain undeveloped… The actual data center footprint will be a fraction of the size of the MIDA project area.” What was actually approved, per the same FAQ on 2026-04-24: The MIDA Board created the Stratos Project Area on April 24 and the Box Elder County Commission agreed to it on May 4. Asked whether those votes approved the full project, the state answers: “No. This is just the beginning of a multi-step process.” Eagle Mountain city land area: 50.4 square miles of land — 32,256 acres — against the 40,000 of the Stratos project area. Rezone the land known as QTS-SCL 2 on 2026-03-03, vote #1046: The most recent data center land vote here, and it states neither acreage nor zoning — which is why nothing local answers a question about size. Last checked 2026-08-19.

docs.title: Contact, corrections and submissions
docs.text: Corrections, questions and submissions go to civicrollcall@gmail.com. That is the only contact route for Civic Roll Call, and it is the address on the about page and on the claims page. Use it to report an error in a figure, a vote or a summary, to point out a meeting that is missing, or to send a claim that is circulating so it can be checked against the record. A report that names the page and the figure, or the meeting date, is the easiest to trace back to the source document. Errors get fixed rather than argued with, and where a correction changes something a reader may already have relied on, the change is noted on the page rather than made silently. Civic Roll Call is published by an Eagle Mountain resident, independently. It is independent of Eagle Mountain City, is not affiliated with any candidate or campaign, carries no advertising and sells nothing; it is not the city, so it cannot take utility, permit or other city business — those go to Eagle Mountain City itself.
